title: Modules II, part 4: module-typed functions and generative escape
body:
Fourth and last of the stack, on top of #2495. Functions take and return modules with abstract types; a path cannot escape the scope of its root.

- **Avoidance.** `Typ.avoid` runs at function bodies, `let` bodies (so `module … in` too) and each `case` arm. A module path rooted at the binder going out of scope is first reduced in the body's context, so a manifest member simply expands. A path that is still abstract stays abstract as an escaped type (see below), except that a signature member defined as that path becomes abstract and later members refer to it by name. So `fun (m : S) -> m` has type `S -> S`, `fun (m : S) -> m.x` has an escaped abstract type as its result, and each call of a function returning a module with abstract members yields a fresh type (generativity). Inside the scope `m.x : m.T` is unchanged; the part-3 tests that pinned root types now read the in-scope type from the info map.
- **Sibling paths.** The signature walk binds value member names as well, so a member typed by a sibling module's abstract type projects as `M.Inner.T` instead of silently becoming `?`. A written-out signature left behind by a type alias (`{ type T = Int }.T`) also projects.
- **Runtime.** A cast to an abstract path type is a no-op: elaboration normalizes manifest paths away, so a path reaching the runtime is abstract. Before, `let z : m.U = m.y` left the stuck value `1:m.U`.
- **Editor.** Deleting the `=` of a signature `type T = Int` downgrades the tile to the bare abstract form (the inverse of part 3's upgrade), leaving the old definition dangling as a stray type to remove or reattach by retyping `=`. `Editing.SigAbstract` grows to 34 cases: typing the bare form, adding `=` in every position, removing it backward, forward and by selection, round trips, and a MakeTerm-level check of the resulting item kinds.
- **Property test.** The QCheck AST generator emits signature types (with a shrinker), and a new property checks that no binder inside a random program leaks into its root type.

**Doc slide.** The split into `modules.hz` and `module-signatures.hz` now lands in part 3; this part adds section G (module-typed functions) to the second slide. Background: adding that section to the combined slide overflowed the JavaScript stack in the CLI. It is not a loop: statics in jsoo overflows node's default stack at roughly 100 plain nested `let`s (about 10 to 16KB per level), and the combined slide had about 70 nesting levels plus 30 `module` bindings. The C3 build needed a stack between 950 and 984KB for it and this one between 984 and 1000KB, against a default of 984KB. The slide is now two: `modules.hz` (construction, qualified types, signatures, errors) and `module-signatures.hz` (width subtyping, abstract types, module-typed functions), both registered in `Slides.re`. The stack depth itself deserves an issue.

## Avoidance keeps the type abstract

Where a path outlives its root, avoidance used to fall back to unknown, and
unknown is consistent with everything, so the loss was silent: nothing told
the author, and every later use checked against nothing. It now mints an
escaped abstract type (`Typ.Escaped`), which is consistent with `?` and with
itself and inconsistent with everything else. That is the relation an
in-scope abstract member already has, so no new rule is invented; what is new
is a representation that survives the loss of its root, generalizing the
clause avoidance already had for signature members.

```
let get = fun (m : BOX) -> m.x in get(B) + 1
-- This has the abstract type m.T, which escaped the scope of its module,
   so it cannot be used where a concrete type is required

let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in dup(ShowInt, "s")
-- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that type;
   mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest signature,
   to keep the caller's type
```

Binding an escaped value, passing it to an unannotated function and giving it
to a hole all still work: the error appears where the author wrote something
concrete, which is the gradual half of the bargain.

- **The parameter is closed too.** The function arm avoided only its body, so
  a component annotated with an earlier component's member left the type
  mentioning a binder no caller can name, and every argument passed, since
  normalization maps a path with an unbound root to unknown. Only the copy
  that becomes the function's type is closed; the pattern's own type and the
  elaborated ascription keep the precise path, so runtime casts and
  incremental-evaluation keys do not move.
- **Generative per application.** `Typ.freshen_escaped` gives each call its
  own identity, so two calls of one function escape different types and
  joining them is an error, while a value bound once and used twice is fine.
  Identities are derived from the application's id rather than generated, so
  re-checking an elaboration still yields an equal type.
- **`Mark.EscapedType` says which side escaped**, so the advice fits the
  case, and an escaped type displays as its path plus a short tag of its
  identity, since two escapes of one path are different types. A failed
  implicit resolution keeps erasing to unknown (`Typ.escape_to`): that
  failure is already marked, and opacity there would only cascade.
- **Not fixed here:** what the caller knows, that the parameter is a
  particular module, still cannot be written in an ordinary arrow type. An
  implicit binder can hold it (#2508); an ML sharing constraint for ordinary
  module parameters is the missing feature. A tuple argument also still
  reports the component and the tuple, which is the pre-existing cascade
  fixed off-stack in #2502.

Two commits: the type form, inert, with its `meet` rules and traversals; then
minting, the closed parameter, freshening and the diagnostics. The escape
tests in the modules suite now assert the escaped type where they asserted
unknown, five new cases cover the behavior, slide item 42 keeps its abstract
type and 43 shows the error.

## Fixes the fuzz properties turned up

Three defects, each found only through a Slow-tagged QCheck property and so only on seeds that generated the shape — parts 5-8 went red while this part stayed green on the very same bugs. Each now has a deterministic test, so the seeds no longer decide.

- **A cyclic alias crashed the analysis.** `type x = x.a in ?` aborted with `weak_head_normalize exceeded 1000 recursive calls`. `TyAlias` already guards self-reference by wrapping the definition in `Rec`, and normalization leaves a `Rec` alone — but from this part `x.a` is a module member projection, so normalizing it asks `path_sig`, and `as_sig` unrolls that `Rec` looking for a signature, handing the projection straight back. Out of fuel the type now comes back unreduced, stuck, which is what the function already returns for everything else it cannot reduce; the program reports `Expected a module or tuple type, found type rec x -> x.a`. `Typ.CyclicAlias` pins it.
- **A printed `:` glued to a leading-plus sum.** `Menhir and maketerm are equivalent` failed on `(()) @< ({ let _:+ Adid }) >`: `:` is an operator character and `Token.is_potential_operator` matches any run of them, so `:+` lexes as one token that is no form at all, while Menhir's separate lexer splits it. `should_add_space` already knew this hazard, but as a list of two characters (`$`, `!`) rather than the property they share; it now asks `Token.begins_with_potential_operator`, which covers `!` along with every other operator character. `$` stays listed, being a name character. An unparenthesized sum only ever reaches a `:` as a sig member's ascription, which is why this appears here.
- **Printing was not idempotent.** `type T = { … }` printed as `({ … })`, then `(({ … }))`, a layer per trip. `parenthesize_typ`'s `Parens` case ran its own content through `paren_typ_at(Precedence.min)`; precedences count down from `max = 0`, so that test wraps exactly the types whose precedence *is* `min` — a Sig, a bare sum, a multihole — and re-wrapped them every pass. The wrapper being emitted is already the protection: nothing outside can bind into it. **Not specific to modules** — `dev` grows the same layers on a parenthesized bare sum (`type T = (+ Adid) in 7`), so this fixes that too and carries it along with the stack.

## Known gaps

- **No dependent domain for ordinary module parameters.** An explicit
  parameter cannot be named later in its own parameter list or in the result
  type, which is exactly the equation this PR reports the loss of. An
  implicit binder (#2508) is the only construct that can hold it, so marking
  the parameter implicit is the current substitute for a sharing constraint.
- **No existentials with an unpacking form.** An escaped abstract type is now
  a real type rather than unknown, but there is no way to give one a name and
  use it, so such a value stays inert. Storing modules with differing
  abstract members in a list, or returning one from a conditional, therefore
  still loses the shared type.

## Verification

title: Modules II, part 8: modular implicits (proof of concept, not close to done)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> **This is a proof of concept and is not close to done.** It is not intended to
> merge as it stands. Its purpose is to show that modular implicits fit Hazel's
> module system and to make one design concrete enough to argue about. The
> syntax, the resolution rule and the error reporting should all be expected to
> change. Please read "Known gaps" at the bottom before reviewing anything else,
> and treat everything above it as a sketch rather than a proposal.

Eighth of the stack, on top of #2503. A function parameter component can be
declared implicit, and a call that leaves it out has it filled in by the type
checker from the instances in scope.

```
type SHOW = { type T; let show : T -> String } in
let implicit ShowInt = { type T = Int; let show = string_of_int } in
let implicit ShowBool = { type T = Bool; let show = fun b -> if b then "true" else "false" } in
let show = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> S.show(x) in
   -- show : (implicit S : SHOW, S.T) -> String
show(3) ++ show(true)     -- "3true": S resolved to ShowInt, then ShowBool
show(ShowBool, true)      -- passed by hand: the arity includes S
```

## What it does

- `implicit S : SIG` is a pattern form (`Pat.Implicit`) and, in an arrow
  domain, a type form (`Typ.Implicit`). Functions stay uncurried: the binder is
  a component of the parameter, and it scopes over the later components and the
  codomain, so `(implicit S : SHOW, S.T) -> String` is an ordinary arrow type.
- `let implicit M = ...`, and the same as a module item, declare an instance
  (`Ctx.ImplicitEntry`). Only such bindings take part in resolution. A binder is
  itself an instance inside the function body, so implicit functions compose.
- At a call, arity decides: the explicit arity resolves every implicit, the full
  arity passes them by hand, and a mix is disambiguated by signature. Resolution
  keeps the instances whose type fits the signature, then narrows by the
  explicit arguments' types and the expected type. One left is the instance;
  none or several is a mark on the application, with a hole passed in the
  instance's place so evaluation proceeds around the error.
- The instance is spliced into the elaborated argument, so the runtime sees an
  ordinary application and the stepper shows `show(ShowInt, 3)`.
- A failed resolution names what the call required, not just the signature:
  `No implicit instance of SHOW with T = String for S`.

New module `src/language/statics/Implicits.re` holds the resolution; `docs/modules.md`
has a section on it, and the new "Module Implicits" doc slide is the worked example.

## Known gaps

Design questions left open, roughly in the order I would want them settled:

1. **Gradual typing weakens resolution.** An instance member written without an
   annotation types as `? -> String`, which fits every `{ let show : X -> String }`,
   so instances become interchangeable and calls turn ambiguous. The workaround
   in the docs (annotate members, use a manifest `type T = E.T`) is a workaround,
   not an answer. This is the part I trust least.
2. **A plain module parameter still loses the caller's type equation**, though
   it no longer loses it silently. #2498 now closes the parameter as well as
   the body, so the same program is an error rather than an unchecked call:

   ```
   let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in
   let out : (String, String) = dup(ShowInt, 3) in out
   -- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that type;
      mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest signature

   let dup = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> (x, x) in
   let out : (String, String) = dup(ShowInt, 3) in out
   -- error: Expecting type String, String but got inconsistent type
      ShowInt.T, ShowInt.T
   ```

   An implicit binder is the only type in the language that can hold what the
   caller knows, which is why the second version checks and the first only
   reports its loss. Marking the parameter implicit is a workaround; the fix
   is a dependent domain for ordinary module parameters, the way Scala's
   dependent method types work, reusing the scoping and substitution this PR
   adds, or an ML sharing constraint. Three tests in
   `Test_Statics_Implicits` pin both halves.


3. **Error attribution.** Both resolution marks sit on the application. That was
   a deliberate choice and it still reads oddly in at least one case on the doc
   slide. Narrowing also runs only when more than one candidate fits the
   signature, so a single unfitting instance reports an argument mismatch
   (`expecting ShowInt.T, got String`) instead of a missing instance. The
   candidate list in an error is every instance in scope rather than the ones
   that fit the signature, and the ambiguity message never says that nothing in
   the call constrained the binder.
4. **No implicit functors.** Instances cannot themselves take implicit
   parameters, so there is no `SHOW` for `[T]` derived from `SHOW` for `T` and no
   recursive search. That is the main thing modular implicits are for, and it is
   entirely absent.
5. **Not supported anywhere else.** `DeferredAp` with implicit components;
   resolving an implicit function that is merely mentioned rather than applied;
   any spelling of `module implicit M : S = ...`.
6. **Cost.** The argument is type-checked twice at an implicit call (a probe pass
   decides the arity), so those applications pay double.
7. **Syntax warts.** `implicit` is now a keyword. A lone
   `implicit S : SIG -> τ` needs parentheses in both the editor and the text
   grammar. The keyword needs two different tile shapes, one per sort, for
   precedence reasons.
8. **Type equality is inconsistent about binder names.** `meet`/`ana_meet`
   rename binders positionally, while `Equality` and `equal_up_to_aliases`
   compare them literally, so `fast_equal` distinguishes types that are
   consistent.
9. **No instance coherence check.** Nothing notices that two instances
   overlap; you find out at a call site, as an ambiguity. A canonicity or
   orphan rule would move that error to the declaration, where it belongs.

Two pre-existing bugs are fixed on the way, both in commit 1: the editor read
`A -> M.T` as `(A -> M).T` because the type-level dot bound looser than the
arrow, and the pattern-annotation printer was not idempotent (`x:(S.T)`
reprinted as `x:((S.T))`).

title: Hazel HTML
body:
Elm-style web apps as Hazel programs. Write a 4-tuple `(init, update, view, subs)` anywhere in a program, project it, and it runs:

```
type Action = Int in
let update(model: Int, action: Action): (Int, Cmd) = (model + action, CmdNone) in
let view(model: Int): HTML =
  Div([], [Button([OnClick(1)], [Text("+")]), Int(model)]) in
(0, update, view, fun _ -> SubNone)
```

Editing `update` while it runs rebinds the live app and keeps its state, as long as the new `view` still accepts the old model.

`HTML`, `Attr`, `Cmd`, `Sub` and `KeyEvent`/`MouseEvent` are builtin types; `HazelDOM` renders values of them to vdom. App state lives in `AppStore`, an id-keyed store in page state rather than in the syntax — models hold closures, and `SetModel` is an edit action, so putting it in the tree would mean whole-document statics per message. Dispatch is `is_edit=false` and non-historic, so clicking a button doesn't touch statics or undo.

The model comes first in `update`, matching `fold_left`'s `(acc, elem)` and Hazel's subject-first convention, so `update` folds directly over a list of actions. `update` always returns `(Model, Cmd)`; a program that issues no commands can return a bare `Model` and lift it with a two-line `noCmd` at the tuple, which keeps the 4-tuple's shape uniform. (The runtime tolerates a bare model via a warning fallback, but relying on it would put two `update` types through one slot.)

There is one HTML projector, not two. It picks its commit target per render from the projected expression's live value: a 4-tuple gets **state** commit, where the model lives in `AppStore`; bare HTML gets **syntax** commit, where the expression itself is the model and an action is an `Html -> Html` transform spliced back in. So "self-modifying HTML" is not a separate feature, just what the projector does when handed HTML — and it only works on closed HTML, since evaluation erases variables before the splice.

To facilitate displaying HTML apps alongside code, all projectors gain a generic placement toggle (`Inline | Sidebar`): Alt+S on any projector docks it to a new Projectors panel, leaving a chip at the code site.

Ten example apps in `hazel-programs/mvu/`, each also shipping as a documentation slide under **MVU / …** with its app already running and docked. `regen-slides.sh` re-encodes the slides from the `.hz` sources; nothing detects a stale encoding, so that script is the only correct way to edit them. The generated slides in `src/mvu/` are most of this PR's diff — ~54k lines, in line with the existing `src/b2t2` (5.8 MB) and `src/web/init/docs` (1.3 MB) slide libraries.

Also here because the ~50-variant recursive builtin types made it necessary: `ConstructorMap.venn_regions` was O(n^2), builtin constructor annotations now stay in compact `Var` form instead of expanding, and physical-equality fast paths were added to `Typ.meet`/`normalize`/`Equality`.

`docs/mvu.md` is the feature doc: program shape, the type and event reference, the design decisions and the known limitations.

Known caveats: `init` accepts any `Var`/`Ap` (the value can only be checked after evaluation), so the HTML context-menu entry offers itself broadly; `AppStore.gc` is implemented but unwired; the Projectors panel shows only the reported editor's projectors; subscriptions are torn down and recreated on every model change, so timers restart their countdown each tick. Opening a slide shows the code plus a chip, and the app appears once the Projectors panel is revealed — the panel choice then persists, so that is one click per browser profile rather than per slide.

Not caused by this branch but worth flagging, since interactive apps make it visible: an MVU dispatch is dominated by `IncrEval.remove_pat_bindings` (~50%) and UUID minting during evaluation (~30%). Measured, with a writeup, but untouched here.

title: User-defined livelits
W2: worker-resident program segments (stacked on modular-editors)
body:
## Goals

Stacked on `modular-editors` (#2469) — review the diff against that base, not dev. This is the experimental next stage of the same perf program: move semantic computation (statics, elaboration, eval bookkeeping) off the UI thread entirely, so the main thread retains only what keystroke latency needs. Everything here is flag-gated and off by default — including shadow mode itself, as of the review fixes (it duplicates statics derivation and worker messaging, so it is a development diagnostic: `__w2shadowToggle(true)` enables it, `__w2flip(true)` implies it). The branch exists to de-risk the architecture with parity evidence before any flip.

## What's here

- **Segment-residency protocol**: the worker holds its own copy of the program segment and applies the same edit deltas the main thread does, so semantic requests ship deltas rather than documents. A headless loopback harness parity-gates worker-side state against the main thread's.
- **Shadow mode**: the app runs the worker pipeline alongside the main-thread one and compares summaries, counting mismatches (`SUMMARY MISMATCH` console reports). This is diagnostic scaffolding, deliberately noisy.
- **Budgeted synchronous statics**: a small time-budgeted synchronous statics pass for the caret's item only, so type-directed feedback at the caret stays immediate even when full statics moves to the worker.
- **Worker summary payload + consumer flip**: the view-side consumers can read statics summaries from the worker instead of the main thread, behind a runtime toggle (`__w2flip`).
- **Instrumentation**: `__staticsProf` per-phase statics-tick diagnostics (gated, zero-cost off); `Test_SerBench` serialization-cost harness (temporary, for the persistence sizing decisions).

## Status / caveats for review

- Codex review findings 1–6 are addressed in `d59762623c`: Resident evals are generation-gated (a rejected delta can no longer evaluate the old program under the new generation's label), recovery is immediate and restart-proof (cached authoritative Full resync on NeedResync and on worker restart, before any retried eval posts), flip toggles bust every DefStatics cache (`reset_caches`), summary grafts update the keyed cache entry and schedule a recalculate (durable + observable), and shadow mode defaults off. Gates in `Test_W2Protocol`.
- Shadow mode (when enabled) reports summary mismatches on some documents; under investigation — treat the comparison logic itself as review-worthy (false positives are as plausible as real divergence).
- The residency protocol's delta-application path remains the highest-value review target: it must reproduce main-thread edit semantics exactly (the loopback parity gate covers what it covers, no more).

title: Modular editors
body:
## Goals

Two thrusts, deliberately on one branch because they feed each other:

1. **Outline mode + stacked subeditors** as a UI feature: navigate a large program by its structure (modules / definitions / types / tests as a collapsible outline) and edit any definition in a small focused cell while whole-program semantics (results, tests, probes) stay live.
2. **Editor performance**, aimed at concrete editing metrics — per-keystroke latency, held-key throughput, worst-case action spikes, slide switching, reload, and autosave cost — across several modes and use cases: flat editing of large programs, stacked/outline editing, and documentation-style slide decks.

The perf work is not incidental: the stacked UI is only viable if editing a 1k–4k-line program is responsive, so most of the pipeline (statics, parse, remold/regrout, view, persistence) was made incremental along the way.

## Try it

Open Documentation → Mega 1k (a ~1,000-line, 10-module program), click `running_sum` in the outline sidebar, and just that definition opens as an editor: typing costs 40–120ms per keystroke while the whole program's result, tests, and probes stay live below the stack. The same program is unusable to edit on dev. For raw-scale editing, the Documentation → "Perf /" folder has Mega 1k/2k/4k flat slides.

## Outline view

- **Outline sidebar**: modules/definitions/types as a collapsible, resizable tree; error badges attach to the deepest visible row and roll up onto collapsed ancestors; erroring names tint red.
- **Stacked per-definition editors**: clicking ⊙ opens a definition as a header cell (`name : type`, pat-rooted) plus a body cell, stacked in program order with module-path qualifier chips. Contexts are frozen at the definition and refreshed when upstream exports change, so cross-definition renames error their dependents live.
- **Whole-program semantics while stacked**: the master keeps evaluating the spliced program — result strip and test results below the stack, and probes sample even when every call site is outside the open cell (samples appear on placement, no follow-up edit needed).
- **Navigation**: jump-to-definition works across cells (opens the target and aligns it only if it isn't already visible); arrow keys walk the caret seamlessly across header/body/cell boundaries and between stacked panes.
- **Structural ops**: right-click an outline row for new definition / new type / new module below, duplicate, move up/down, delete — segment surgery on the live program, so unchanged definitions keep their ids (open cells and probes stay pinned). Ops cost the changed item plus its downstream users, not the program (mega-2k: ~3s → ~220–260ms steady-state; the term itself is parsed per item and grafted — `MakeTerm.Incr`, exact-parity test-gated). With a cell open at mega-2k, an idle 8s window has zero long tasks.
- **Tests, statements, and trailing bodies in the outline — in every block**: `test …;` statements get rows with live ✓/✗ icons at any depth (module-member tests included), other `…;` statements get `;` rows, and trailing bodies get `⇒` rows — each opens as a headerless cell.
- **Pins and collapse persist** per slide, across slide switches and reloads (name-anchored via outline label paths); collapse is modeled state, so folding no longer bleeds between slides or resets on structural edits.
- **Structural ops at every level**: the row context menu works on module members and function-body items too — inserts mint proper member forms inside modules — and moves stay within their block.
- **Headers got real**: cell statics are projected from the whole-program per-item analysis (one statics run, cells read it) — unannotated headers show their inferred types, module headers have live statics, unused-binder warnings reach headers.
- **Statics in every cell kind**: expression bodies, type-alias bodies, and pat/tpat headers all get cursor-inspector info and sort-correct coloring.
- **Persistence**: autosave is per-item serialized (`ItemPersist`): each top-level item's segment is stored as its own sexp under an ordered roster — the edited item's write is ~3–10ms — and reload restores the segment exactly, incomplete tiles included, with no text parse. A content-changing pause additionally rewrites the whole-document text blob (schema-drift fallback), which keeps an O(document) print on the autosave path (~11ms at 1k / ~27ms at 4k in the headless SerBench harness); making that blob per-item too is an open follow-up. Caret survives reloads via a side key.

## Performance

- **Compositional statics** (`DefStatics`): whole-program statics computed per top-level item with chained contexts; a typical edit re-analyzes the dirty set — the edited item plus export-affected dependents, e.g. 16 of 891 items (56ms headless) on a surgical 4k edit vs 872ms for the cold pass. Member-granular items inside module literals analyze per member. Fixes the browser stack-overflow crash that made mega-2k unloadable. Parity with monolithic statics is test-gated (errors, grafted-elaboration eval, probe capture). Per-document LRU slots make returning to a slide a warm lookup instead of a full cold re-analysis.
- **Sparse remold/regrout** (`Segment`/`Zipper`): remold short-circuits on same-mold tiles; regrout runs only on a caret window whose extent is derived from a read-only normal-form scan, memoized by tile identity — the remold/regrout phase drops from ~1.2s per 60 keystrokes at 4k lines to ~1ms/action. Parity-gated: the test runner executes both the sparse and the global pipeline on every call and asserts equivalence across the whole suite.
- **Read-free caret reveal** (`CaretReveal`): scroll-into-view no longer forces layout on every keystroke — the caret decoration publishes its model-side row geometry; during typing bursts the reveal is pure arithmetic against mirrored scroll state, with a same-frame rAF anchor read only on cold (post-pause) reveals and a throttled heal for drift. Held-key benchmarks at 4k: enter p95/max 550/936 → 133/448, letter 367/960 → 200/360.
- **Identity-preserving splices**: stacked-mode edits re-mint only the changed item's pieces, which is what makes the per-item dirty tracking (statics, persistence, vdom) actually fire; plus cached stacked parse and outline vdom memo for the stacked-mode edit spikes.
- **Incremental view**: chunked measurement and per-chunk content-keyed vdom — 4k flat edit ~1.6s → ~100ms attributable; 2k edit 690 → ~53ms.
- **Text round-trip for operator holes**: the printer now spells concave grout ⧖ (convex stays ¿), so documents containing infix holes survive text persistence without hitting the quadratic recovering parser (previously a multi-minute reload at ~27k chars). Lexer/parser support landed separately on dev (#2479); this branch carries the integration.
- **Worker-resident incremental eval cache / streaming overhaul / memory fixes**: unchanged from the earlier description — request payloads no longer ship the previous cache; incremental stream collector (parity-gated); exponential co_ctx leak fixed; undo snapshots compacted; render-generation closure chain broken. Mega-2k slide open: ~47s main-thread busy → ~3s.

## Review notes

The design docs live in a gitignored `plans/` tree, so this description is the context. Recent, least-reviewed range: `9c24363bcc..8e0c9d7dbc` (sparse regrout, caret reveal, per-item persistence, ⧖ integration); older subsystems have had more soak time.

Codex review findings 1–3 are addressed in `29b726d3c8` (occurrence-qualified sexp-encoded outline paths, content-key-tagged pending restore state, CaretReveal single listener + caret-identity anchoring), with gates in `Test_OutlinePaths`.

Where extra scrutiny would help most:
- `src/haz3lcore/tiles/Segment.re` — the normal-form scan (`stale_in_seg`/`stale_affix_ids`) and its identity memo (global id-keyed table, pointer-validated, 200k cap): memo soundness and multi-editor sharing.
- `src/haz3lcore/zipper/Zipper.re` — `split_window`/`window_bound`: the caret-window bounds for sparse regrout (the window bound is deliberately the boundary solid's shape *complement*; threading the true shape double-decides out-of-scope runs).
- `src/haz3lcore/zipper/ItemPersist.re` + `src/web/view/ScratchPersist.re` — write ordering (items → roster → GC), load fallback on any inconsistency, and the root-repair path.
- `src/util/CaretReveal.re` — mirrored scroll geometry and the WAAPI-vs-CSS animation filtering (the caret's CSS blink must not pin reveals cold).
- `src/haz3lcore/derived/DefStatics.re` — `head_equal` uses polymorphic compare on term heads; derived stable ids for mod-item wrappers; LRU keying by whole-term rep id.

Deliberate decisions (please don't re-litigate without a failure case): the whole-text autosave blob is kept as schema-drift fallback alongside the per-item sexps; parity gates for sparse regrout stay enabled in the test runner; DOM virtualization is planned but explicitly not built (the remaining 4k spikiness is GC + per-key view floor, semantics-independent).

Known follow-ups: stepper while stacked, projector sidebar apps while stacked, worker-resident program segments (stacked PR: w2-worker-residency), hierarchical (sub-item) chunking and persistence for huge single items, episodic eval frame at 4k.

title: Stack overflow crash on programs nested ~125 deep (e.g. 125 let-in lines)
body:
Pasting this into an empty scratch editor on https://hazel.org/build/dev/ (Chrome) shows the crash page "Exception during Calculate: Stack overflow":

```
let a0 = 0 in
let a1 = 1 in
...
let a124 = 124 in
a0
```

Generate it with `python3 -c "print('\n'.join(f'let a{i} = {i} in' for i in range(125)) + '\na0')" | pbcopy`, then Cmd+V. 100 lines works; 125 crashes about a second after the paste. `1 + (1 + (1 + ...` nested 150 deep crashes the same way, while a flat program of the same size (a 1000-element list literal, ~2000 tokens) is fine, so the trigger is nesting depth, not program size. Typing or loading such a program hits it too, since every edit re-runs the same pass.

A CPU profile at the crash shows the segment-to-term pass recursing three frames per nesting level (`MakeTerm.go_s` → `unsorted` → `exp`); the frames are large enough that ~125 levels exhaust Chrome's ~1 MB main-thread stack. The `--profile dev` build crashes at ~100 levels, and the CLI already needs `node --stack-size=8192` for the same reason. The modular-editors branch happens to survive 200 nested `let`s because it parses each definition separately, but nested parentheses would still overflow there. Not bisected.

title: Concave-grout marker: round-trip operator holes as ⧖
body:
Concave grout printed as `¿`, the same marker as convex grout, so persisted text was ambiguous — and a text-persisted document with an infix hole hit the slow recovering parser on every reload, because `1 ¿ 2` lexes as three operands.

Concave grout now prints as `⧖` (U+29D6) and round-trips through the fast path: lexer token, identifier-class carve-out (same pattern as `¿`), and a `BinHole` production in every sort the editor molds it for — Exp, Pat (including fun parameters), Typ (including fun-parameter ascriptions) and TPat.

Precedence follows the editor's `Precedence.concave_grout`: looser than every binary operator, tighter than `;` and the let/fun/if/case bodies, so `let x = 1 in x ⧖ 2` keeps the hole in the body and `(Int -> Bool) ⧖ String` reduces the arrow first. To express the latter with one token, the arrow-bodied binders (`fun`/`fix`/`typfun`, `poly`/`rec`) take their own `BINDER_BODY` level instead of the arrow token's; their behaviour is otherwise unchanged (the existing Menhir/fuzz/corpus suites pass as before).

Conversion flattens a parsed chain into one flat `MultiHole` and prints a uniform-sort `MultiHole` back as a chain; mixed-sort holes have no textual spelling and stay on the slow path.

Base-type keywords (`Int`, `Bool`, `String`, …) are now constructor patterns in Menhir as they already were in exp position: deleting the arrow in `let x : Int -> Bool` leaves a pattern-level hole beside `Bool`, and that document (and plain `let Bool = 1`) used to fall to the recovering parser on every load.

Gates: `TextRoundtrip.EditedGrout` — 12 programs where grout is left by simulated typing (not hand-written markers) in every sort: the persisted text must fast-parse, keep its grout through the load-time regrout, and reprint as a fixed point. `MenhirParser.ConcaveMarker` — 33 cases pinning Menhir ≡ MakeTerm through the marker load path (`MarkerParse.of_text`, where the marker becomes real grout) across all four sorts — and `TextRoundtrip.ConcaveMarker` (14 fast-parse/fixed-point cases incl. legacy `¿` canonicalization). One divergence class is deliberately not pinned: the sort tag MakeTerm gives a hole's neighbour (`let x : Int ⧖ y` sorts `y` as a type, Menhir as a pattern — same structure, same tokens).

Grammar conflicts: +1 s/r state and +1 r/r state over dev, both in the documented families (UNIT lookahead after `pat ⧖ pat`; funAscAtom sharing nonAscriptingPat), listed in the grammar's KNOWN CONFLICT FAMILIES comment.

title: Statics: a capitalized name resolves to its most recent binding (module vs constructor)
body:
```
type T = + Text + Other in
module Text = { let f = fun n -> "x" } in
Text.f(0) == "x"
```
This reports "Expected a tuple" at `Text.f`. A capitalized name parses as a constructor and statics looked it up constructor-first, falling back to a variable binding only when no constructor of that name existed anywhere. So a module named like any constructor in scope lost to it, no matter which was bound later.

This PR makes the most recent binding of the name win, whichever kind it is (`Ctx.newest_var_or_ctr`), which is what shadowing means for every other name. Expression position only; constructor patterns are unchanged. Draft because the rule deserves a careful look: it changes what a capitalized identifier means when a module and a constructor share a name.

title: Make tiles slightly less illegal
body:
Tiles stored their label and mold even though both are determined by form. Each serialized tile carried redundant strings and precedence numbers so operator-precedence changes required migrating every serialized file, and nothing prevented label/mold mismatches.

Now a tile is `{id, form, sort, shards, children}` where `form = Compound(family) | Tok(token) | TokInfix(token)`, with 92 form families (label x shape-role) plus free-text tokens, and label/mold are derived. `TokInfix` is a technical detail that will die with virtual grout.

This isn't quite a pure refactor, but my hope is that there are no observable logic changes.

- Serialized syntax shrinks ~40%, and precedence/mold changes no longer require migrations.
- MakeTerm dispatches on constructors instead of token-string lists. This technically causes some behavior changes in edge cases, but I have never seen the relevant behaviors in the wild.
- Exercise/derivation examples now ship as serialized-zipper text literals rather than OCaml literals, so they survive representation changes; slide files were regenerated id- and refractor-preservingly.
- The stored `sort` is an explicitly isolated local cache (well-sorted <=> `mold_of(form, sort).out == sort`); experimental follow up work will hopefully make sort a derived property, eliminating this field
- The grammar's string layer now lives in the language library (src/language/grammar/), including Token, Label, and FormId (the family enums and the per-family label table), following the existing Sort re-export pattern. This deduplicates the token/string mirrors that src/language previously hand-maintained
- TyDi's suggestion-type tables are now derived from the grammar at startup instead of hand-maintained.

title: Semantic Scaffolding
body:
Typing `(1, ` where a 3-tuple is expcted owes a comma and a closer: this branch derives those obligations from statics, shows them as quiver chips or inline ghosts (when the caret is at the completion site), reifies them into the analyzed program, and Tab-accepts them progressively.

Stacked on completion-provenance (#2374). 

This also consolidates previous completion-oriented code into one system (one completed segment drives statics and display), replacing the  selection-buffer machinery previously used by TyDi.

title: Hazel in Patchwork
body:
## Try it out:

1. Go to [patchwork.inkandswitch.com](https://patchwork.inkandswitch.com).
2. Go to 'My tools' in the Patchwork sidebar, and select 'Register a Module'. Enter the following module URL: `automerge:27ShjXmwBQPAovhh9Sgd5L5ue1a1`. This registers a HazelDoc Patchwork datatype and tool, which will enable you to create and view new HazelDocs.
3. Go to 'Create new' in the Patchwork sidebar, and select 'New HazelDoc'.
4. This may be set to try and load Hazel locally by default; click the 'Remote' button on the lowest top bar to set the Hazel URL to the patchwork branch on the hazel build server.
5. At this point, you should see a hazel scratchpad, possibly in Patchwork-enforced Dark Mode, depending on your system settings
6. You should be able to share this doc with others by selecting 'Copy share URL' in the `...` menu at the top right. 

----------------------------------------------------------

## Relevant external URLs:

- Patchwork: [patchwork.inkandswitch.com](https://patchwork.inkandswitch.com).
- HazelDoc Patchwork plugin source: See our [patchwork-extra fork](https://github.com/hazelgrove/patchwork-extra/tree/hazel/hazel) here. This will need to be built and redeployed via `patchwork push` if changes are made; see [patchwork-integration.md](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/blob/patchwork/docs/patchwork-integration.md) in the docs directory for detailed instructions.
- HazelDoc module Automerge URL: `automerge:27ShjXmwBQPAovhh9Sgd5L5ue1a1`

----------------------------------------------------------
## Hazel in Patchwork

This adds supports for collaborative multiplayer hazel programs via patchwork+automerge.

In particular:
- Hazel programs can be created within Patchwork by adding the HazelDoc tool via its automerge URL.
- These can be shared by generating a Patchwork share link.
- Caret positions are broadcast across all clients, and decorated with patchwork usernames and user color (if logged in). 
- This version of Hazel behaves different when loaded in an iframe, for example by our patchwork tool wrapper. It starts in Zen Mode (hiding the top, bottom, and side bars); press Cmd/Ctrl-K to toggle the rest of the UI. All other editors modes other than a single scratch slide are disabled. Localstorage persistence is disabled in favor of automerge.
- Many kinds of concurrent edits are possible without clobbering other user's edits, however there are rough edges to this and inconsistent states across clients are possible.

Minor limitations:
- Your caret position will be changed if another user makes an edit to the token/delimiter that you're on, or to a selection that contains your caret. Fallback repositioning logic handles many cases well but isn't perfect.
- Similarly, your range selection may be disrupted by other user's edits to pieces around its extremities. In such cases we drop the selection rather than possibly make errors around the edges. Edits contained entirely within a selection usually don't disrupt it though.
- Remote carets are not proactively cleaned up on disconnect and remain for up to 3 minutes if a user drops

Major limitation:
- Hazel's engagement with the automerge CRDT framework is partial. In particular, certain concurrent edits may clobber another user's edits if edits are made within the same 'tile footprint'. This is a slightly subtle notion. One way to mentally approximate is is that concurrent edits can be made without issue inside different top definitions, but concurrently adding top-level definitions, or otherwise concurrently modifying the top level structure, may result in clobbering. Below I'll describe in detail the convex hull of situations where clobbering may occur. However, I have instituted logic to make many such edits compatible with each other, at the cost of making the class of problematic conflicting edits even harder to describe, and likely introducing subtle bugs. To a first approximation though, **the only situations which are currently known to be problematic (in the sense of possibly causing inconsistency, or else certainly causing clobbering) are when two users simultaneously try to edit delimiters of a multi-delimiter form** (say for example given `let x = 1 i` where one user appends and `n` at the same time as another backspaces the `t`. The only other situation which definitely causes clobbering are **when two users edit the same token at the same time**. There's no intrinsic complexity here; we'd just need to switch the token type to the automerge text CRDT; it's just not totally clear to me if that's desirable behavior for all token classes. It might be reasonable for a comment, but when editing a variable name perhaps clobbering is better? Unsure.
 
----------------------------------------------------------

## Appendix: Restructuring operations versus concurrent edits.

**Note: The below is now outdated, after implementing the plan specified in [automerge-granular-sync.md](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/blob/patchwork/docs/automerge-granular-sync.md). However it is retained as an intuition pump for the impedance mismatch which has now been partially addressed. In particular, both of the examples at the end now work fine concurrently**

-  We currently use the automerge CRDT at the level of the piece map; a map from UUIDs to flat syntactic forms, which reference other UUIDs as children. However, these flattened forms are flatter than one might suspect. Instead of containing a list of child UUIDs, they contain a list of lists of UUIDs. Each of the top level lists represents a child, and each of the child lists represents the tiles constituting that child.

For example, consider the following program: 

```
let x = 1 + (2 * 3) in
let y = 4 in
x + y
```

This will have the following (simplified) flattened rep:

```
{
  X: Root([[A, B, C, D, E]]),
  A: Let([[F], [G, H, I]]),
  F: Atom("x"),
  G: Atom("1"),
  H: Atom("+"),
  I: Parens([[J, K, L]]),
  J: Atom("2"),
  K: Atom("*"),
  L: Atom("3"),
  B: Let([[M], [N]]),
  M: Atom("y"),
  N: Atom("4"),
  C: Atom("x"),
  D: Atom("+"),
  E: Atom("y"),
}
```

Our basic setup handles concurrent edits to **individual entries** in the above list, but concurrent edits to the same entry will result in clobbering. So, for example, any two atomic tokens can be concurrently edited. But, any addition to the root segment, for example adding a new let definition (say, for a new variable z) between the two existing one while another user adds a `+ z` to the end of the program, will result in clobbering. Additionally, if a user tries to edit the pattern for the definition of `x`, say changing it to `x, w`, while another user edits the definition similarly, say changing `1 + (2 * 3)` to `1 + (2 * 3), 4`, these will get clobbered because, even though they are not edits to the same segment, they are nonetheless both edits to the **list of lists** for node A.

title: Colors: one semantic vocabulary, from the config slide to the stylesheets
body:
Stacked on #1591 (`configuration`).

The Colors slide's type used to *be* the CSS variable list with Hazel syntax on
it: `expected_type` was generated from lists of raw custom-property names, and
the header said so outright — "The label IS the CSS custom-property name,
verbatim." So a themer edited CSS internals: `BR2`, `T3`, `shard-caret-tpat`,
`GB1`, and a misspelling (`backback-targets`) that was load-bearing because it
was a CSS name.

This gives the theme an explicit, semantic representation and maps it onto CSS,
then collapses the three stacked CSS vocabularies into one.

## What changed

**The shape of a theme is a type.** `BuiltinsColorScheme.re` holds it as Hazel
types in the builtin context — `ColorSeeds`, `ColorPalette`, `ColorRoles`,
`ColorScheme` — and the slide writes them in its own signatures:
`let theme_of(p: ColorPalette, role: ColorOverrides): ColorScheme`.
`ColorRamp`/`ColorOverrides` are declared in the slide, being seams between its
own two functions. That puts each check on the record a mistake is in; without
it the only analysis is the whole-program one, which lands on the final `case`
as a single inconsistency between two enormous products.

**The slide names roles**, grouped by the part of the UI they dress (`menu`,
`editor`, `cursor`, `hole`, `probe`, …), with a fan-out table in
`ColorConfiguration.re` expanding each field to the CSS properties that carry
it — one field per *decision*, several targets where several properties carry
one decision. ~~`expected_type` and
`all_targets` both derive from that table, so they cannot drift apart.~~
`all_targets` derives from that table; `expected_type` is the named
`ColorScheme`, and a test pins that the slide fills it exactly.

The two layers differ by **reuse, not derivation**: a palette color is one the
theme is built out of, fanned out to several properties at once; a role is one
job a color is put to, usually carrying one. Roles that only forwarded a
stated color are palette entries now, renamed for what they are (`exp-base` →
`probe-value`, `main-base` → `statics-background`).

**~~The palette took the slide's names: `--Y1` → `--attention-2`, `--T1` →
`--surface-1`, `--SAND` → `--code-background`.~~** The rename landed, and then
the names went: nothing read `--ink`, `--frame-1` or the rest — no stylesheet,
no OCaml, no script, and the only references left in the tree were commented
out. A palette color now reaches CSS only under the semantic names the fan-out
gives it, which makes "components consume roles, not the palette" structural
rather than lint-enforced.

**`roles.css` is deleted.** It was a third vocabulary: hand-written aliases
carrying nearly half the component `var()` sites, and its names resolved to far
fewer palette colors than there were names, so `--text-faint`,
`--border-soft` and `--shadow-soft` were one color with no way to separate
them. Every entry was a bare alias, so they fold into the fan-out table and the
theme writes them itself. ~~**No component stylesheet changed** — every site
reads the same names as before.~~ None changed for *that*; elsewhere on the
branch some sites were renamed off the raw palette names.

**`variables.css` has no hand-written color left**: type, timing and the
z-index ladder. ~~Type, a generated block (`make update-css-defaults`, guarded
by a test), and the z-index ladder.~~ The generated defaults are their own
labelled file, `style/theme-generated.css`, byte-identical to what the theme
sets so nothing shifts when it lands.

**The gap is closed.** The colors the theme did not own were dead, pure
indirection, or derived by CSS itself (the `doc` hue rotations, the
`incremental-pending` fades); they are decided in the slide now.

**Two flags, and they compose.** `--hazel-color-scheme` feeds the standard
`color-scheme` property; `--hazel-contrast` is new, so a stylesheet can answer
high contrast with a style query. Four schemes from two booleans, one `case`.

**Also fixed:** `color-scheme` was set nowhere, so native scrollbars rendered
light on a dark editor; the two flags overrode each other instead of composing;
`proj-fold.css` had an inert `color: --var(BLACK)`; and table rows and headers
were near-illegible in high contrast, because a row highlight was placed on the
page's contrast axis when table rows sit on the code background.

**The slide reads better.** It opens with every scheme but the first folded;
tuple extension instead of restating records, direct function definitions, and
a smaller `ColorOverrides` — several of its fields turned out to be one
decision spelled a few ways. `style/README.md` is new, and documents the
dataflow, file ownership and both layers.

## How it is checked

- **Golden** (`test/goldens/colors.tsv`): every property × every scheme.
  Written sorted by name, so a pure restructuring leaves it and
  `theme-generated.css` byte-identical — which is how every refactor after the
  vocabulary work was verified.
- **Reverse substitution** for renames: mapping the new names back reproduces
  every touched file byte for byte.
- **Chrome**, at each stage: every variable resolves to the golden in all four
  schemes, and a stylesheet-only page with no JavaScript resolves them all to
  the light column.
- **`./hazel analyze hazel-programs/config/colors.hz`** names the offending
  term when an annotation stops holding.
- `lint_css_roles.py` rewritten for the two-layer shape: components read roles
  not the palette, only the generated file declares a theme-owned color on
  `:root`, and the dangling-reference ratchet stays.

## Known gaps

- Folding kept "one field per decision", so `--text-faint` and `--border-soft`
  still come off one `palette.frame-1` row. Splitting a case is a two-file
  change; a field per property was rejected as worse to read.
- Two further override merges would each move a color by one ramp step, so
  they want an eye rather than a green test: collapsing the `frame-*` dials,
  and merging `projector.textarea-text` into `inspector.text`.
- **TODO:** we still need some way of enforcing that newly added colors stay
  themeable. The lint catches a component declaring a theme-owned color on
  `:root`, but not a new hardcoded literal in a rule.

body: # Configuration Mode Adds a configuration mode to Hazel for editing editor settings as Hazel programs, with two slides: **Colors** (adds dark, high-contrast, and high-contrast dark schemes) and **Shortcuts** (rebinds the command-palette actions). > Screenshot predates the seeds/palette/roles rework and the colour picker — it shows the mode, not the current slide. ## How `ConfigurationMode.re` is split out of `ScratchMode.re`. Each slide is a Hazel program analyzed against a type, read back after evaluation, and applied to the running editor. **Colors** — `hazel-programs/config/colors.hz` is committed Hazel text, embedded at build time with `ppx_blob` the way doc slides are. It layers *seeds* → *palette* → *roles*: ~38 seeds feed a palette, and `style/roles.css` exposes the semantic roles the stylesheets consume. Every `style/*.css` file moved off palette names onto roles, with `make lint-css` (`scripts/lint_css_roles.py`) as the ratchet. `dark_mode` and `high_contrast` are `^^check` flags in the program and they compose: a single `case` on the pair at the bottom selects one of four schemes (light, dark, high-contrast light, high-contrast dark), reading each flag exactly once, so adding a scheme costs one line rather than one conditional per colour. Each scheme carries its own seeds — dark is *not* derivable from light, as most seeds are re-hued. `BuiltinsColor`/`BuiltinsADT`/`BuiltinsBase` add a `ColorValue` type and the colour arithmetic the program needs; `ColorProj.re` puts a direct-manipulation OKLCH picker (with an RGB tab) on every colour literal. **Shortcuts** — `ShortcutAction.re` is a single registry every action flows through, so the slide, the command palette, and the key handling cannot disagree. The slide term is generated from that registry and analyzed against its action set; `KeybindingProj.re` records a binding on click → chord → Escape. Resolved bindings land in `Settings.Model.shortcut_overrides` and are applied when the palette is built. ## Testing `test/ConfigSlideCheck.re` is a shared harness pinning that each slide typechecks against its analyzed type, that the analysis is engaged, and that Colors still evaluates. Plus `Test_Color`, `Test_ColorConfiguration`, `Test_ConfigurationMode`, `Test_ShortcutAction`, `Test_ShortcutConfiguration`. Each of the four colour schemes is evaluated on its own — the slide as committed has both flags false, so only `light` would otherwise be exercised — and pinned pairwise-distinct, which is what catches a flag being ignored. `docs/legacy-{light,dark}-palette.txt` record the hand-written palettes the derivation replaced. ## Issues (to be addressed in future prs) - There's a lot of duplication between configuration mode and scratchmode - The original version had them combined and I split them up. I think we want them to be able to diverge more and need a better story for the common parts between editors. - Colour updates are applied by side effect — `JsUtil.set_css_variable` writes CSS custom properties straight onto `documentElement`. Threading them through the model would mean passing actions up/down the model stack. (Shortcuts do go through the model, via `Settings.Update.SetShortcutOverrides`.) - Stronger analyzed types for these editors — e.g. constraining a role to a colour-valued expression — are still future work. - **TODO: we need some way of enforcing that new colours stay themable.** Nothing currently stops a colour being written straight into a stylesheet, and that is how the un-themable ones accumulated — `make lint-css` checks that roles are bare aliases and ratchets dangling refs, but never asks whether a colour a stylesheet paints is reachable from the theme at all.

title: Term-level refactorings
body:
13 context-menu/palette refactorings built on the round-trip (#2374): parse buffer -> transform term -> print -> splice. Ids survive, so probes, statics, and incremental caches do too.

### Gestural - Naming
- **Inline Let**: `let x = 1 + 2 in x + 3` -> `1 + 2 + 3`; offered at the let, its binder, or any occurrence of `x`. Parens only where a reparse oracle proves the bare form changes the program: `let x = 1 + 2 in 3 + x` -> `3 + (1 + 2)`.
- **Add Parameter**: `let f = fun x -> x + 1 in f(2)` -> `let f = fun (x, x1) -> x + 1 in f(2, ?)` — definition and every call site atomically, including recursive calls. Handles `let f(x) = x + 1 in f(2)` -> `let f(x, x1) = x + 1 in f(2, ?)` and annotated bindings (`Int -> Int` becomes `(Int, ?) -> Int`). Gated off when `f` is used as a bare value (`map(f, xs)`).
- **Hoist Let**: `fun n -> let x = 2 in x + n` -> `let x = 2 in fun n -> x + n` — one level per invocation (through chains, out of defs, out of lambdas). The explicit opt-in to evaluation-count changes that Extract avoids.
- **Sink Let**: `let x = 2 in case m | 1 => x | _ => 0 end` -> `case m | 1 => let x = 2 in x | _ => 0 end` — into the single arm/branch/lambda that uses the binding. Both movements are scope-gated and shadow-aware; blocked moves are simply not offered.
- **Extract to Let**: binds at the nearest enclosing line — `let a = 1 in g(f(2))` extracting `f(2)` -> `let a = 1 in let x = f(2) in g(x)`; a def-site hoists above its line (`let a = g(f(2)) in ...` -> `let x = f(2) in let a = g(x) in ...`). Never escapes a lambda or case arm, so evaluation count/conditionality never changes.

### Gestural - Choice
- **Add Missing Case Arm**: `case b | true => 1 end` -> `case b | true => 1 | false => ? end`, one arm per invocation from the Coverage witness — real constructors for finite domains (`Green`), literals wildified for infinite ones (`case n | 1 => 2 end` gains `| _ => ?`). Label names the witness: "Add Arm | false".

### Naming (non-gestural)
- **Rename (bind free occurrences)**: rename a binder by ordinary editing — `let vel = 1 in v + v` (was `v`) marks the old uses free, and the binder token offers "Rename v to vel" -> `let vel = 1 in vel + vel`. Stateless: reconstructed from scope state, no edit tracking. Works at let heads, `f(x)`-sugar names and params, fun params, and case-arm pats; per-occurrence shadow-precise.
- **Remove Unused Let**: `let x = 1 in 2 + 2` -> `2 + 2`; gated on the statics unused-binding warning. Works on annotated heads and unused `f(x)`-sugar fns.

### Equational (syntactic)
- **Convert to Case**: `if a then 1 else 2` -> `case a | true => 1 | false => 2 end`.
- **Convert to If**: the inverse, either arm order: `case a | false => 2 | true => 1 end` -> `if a then 1 else 2`.
- **Negate & Swap Branches**: `if a && b then 1 else 2` -> `if !(a && b) then 2 else 1` — arms swap with their formatting untouched; condition parens by the oracle (`if a ...` gives bare `!a`).
- **Eta-Reduce**: `fun y -> f(y)` -> `f`, gated on `y` not occurring in `f`.

### Equational (semantic)
- **Add Type Annotation**: `let x = 1 + 2 in x` -> `let x : Int = 1 + 2 in x`, type from statics; only offered when the inferred type is hole-free. Oracle-parenthesized: `let p = (1, true) in p` -> `let p : (Int,Bool) = (1, true) in p`.


Formatting is preserved by construction: whitespace runs belong to line slots and transforms move/copy them explicitly, so multiline layouts survive swaps, extractions, and conversions. Menu gating never prints, parses, or runs the oracle (invocation only). ~110 tests in Test_Refactor.re.

Stacked on #2374; retarget to dev when it merges.

title: Add D3 chart projector (^^chart) with optional auto-display
body:
## Summary

Adds a `^^chart` projector that renders a Hazel value as a chart, modeled on the existing
Table projector. The same labeled-tuple data that feeds tables is naturally chartable, so
this gives bar / grouped-bar / line / scatter / pie views of evaluated results.

Charts are described by a new built-in `Chart` ADT. Rendering is done **by d3 itself** (d3
owns the DOM): the selection/axis/shape code lives in JS, and OCaml recognizes the data and
hands d3 the container node.

## The `Chart` ADT (`BuiltinsADT.re`)

```
type Chart =
  + BarChart([(label=String, value=Float)])
  + GroupedBarChart([(name=String, data=[(label=String, value=Float)])])
  + LineChart([(x=Float, y=Float)])
  + ScatterChart([(x=Float, y=Float)])
  + PieChart([(label=String, value=Float)])
```

Bar/Pie share the categorical shape; Line/Scatter share the points shape; GroupedBarChart is
a list of named series. Constructor names are namespaced (`BarChart`, not `Bar`) to avoid the
flat global constructor namespace (JSON already claims `Float`/`Int`/`String`/`List`/`Bool`).
Registered via a single `type_aliases` row.

Data must be `Float` in the surface language — there is **no implicit `Int`→`Float` coercion**
(use `float_of_int`), matching the ADT's payload types.

## Architecture

- **`ChartCore.re`** — a pure, D3-free recognizer (`parse_chart : Exp.t => option(chart_spec)`),
  reusing `TableCore.parse_table` + `HazelJson`'s wrapper stripping. Unit-tested natively. Also
  exports `is_chart_ctr_ap`, the cheap type-level test that gates auto-display (below).
- **`ChartProj.re`** — marshals `chart_spec` to a JS object and drives d3 through **one generic
  `Attr.create_hook`** (like the existing `ScrollIntoViewHook`). The container `<div>` has no
  vdom children, so vdom leaves d3's subtree alone across re-renders. Mirrors `TableProj` for
  `init`/`get`/`placeholder`/`error`.
- **`prebundle.js`** — `window.HazelD3.render(el, spec)` dispatches on `spec.kind` using real d3
  (`d3.axisLeft`/`axisBottom`, `.data().enter()`, `d3.line`, `d3.pie`/`d3.arc`). Series colors come
  from CSS vars (`--chart-1..8`, an earthy palette in `variables.css`), with native `<title>`
  tooltips, hover highlight, bar value labels, per-series legends, and pie-legend truncation.
- Registered in `ProjectorKind` (`^^chart` via lexer + `of_name`), `ProjectorInit`, context menu.

Adding a chart kind is a `chart_spec` variant + a `js_of_spec` branch + a JS render function.

**Grouped series align by label** ([review](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2350#discussion_r3460638264)):
the category axis is the union of every series' labels in first-seen order, and each series looks
its own values up by label. `series.values : list(option(float))` is positional against that axis,
with `None` crossing to JS as `null` so `renderBar` leaves a gap instead of shifting a series'
remaining bars into another category's slot. Series need not carry the same categories, or the
same number of them.

## Auto-display in eval output (`project_charts` setting)

Mirrors `project_tables`: a `Chart` value in an evaluated result auto-renders when the **"Charts"**
toggle is on (Nut menu → Value Display). No conflict with tables — tables fire on bare list
literals, charts on `Chart`-constructor applications. Off by default (opt-in), like Tables.

The gate is the constructor's **type**, not its name
([review](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2350#discussion_r3431328434)):
`is_chart_ctr_ap` peels arrows off the type statics puts on the constructor and compares the
result against `BuiltinsADT.Chart.t`. Every variant is covered without enumerating names, and a
user ADT that shadows a Chart constructor name is not projected as a chart.

## Testing

- `test/Test_ChartCore.re` (17 cases): all kinds incl. grouped, empty/ragged/non-finite data,
  Int-value rejection, a positional-tuple case verifying the ADT registration drives
  auto-labeling, grouped series with differing and short label lists, and the auto-display gate
  (accepts all five constructors; rejects a shadowed constructor name and unelaborated syntax).
- `make dev` builds clean; `make test-quick` passes (3326 tests).
- Manually verified rendering for every kind in the browser (manual `^^chart` and auto-display).
  The label-union grouped rendering wants one more browser pass.

## Notes / trade-offs

- ~~Grouped/multi-series bars are supported by the recognizer but not reachable through the
  single-value-column ADT… open question whether to add a dedicated grouped-bar constructor.~~
  **Resolved:** added the `GroupedBarChart` constructor (typed, explicit), rendered with
  per-series colors + a legend.
- A multi-numeric-column inner `data` table is unreachable from a well-typed program (the ADT
  types the payload as a single `(label, value)` list), so `parse_grouped` reads the first
  numeric column and says so in a comment rather than guarding it. The multi-column path in

title: Don't reuse a cached value that carries no environment
body:
Fixes #2462.

`IncrEval.reuse_check` could hand back a cached value that was a bare `Fun` — no `Closure`, so no environment. Applying it then lands in `Transition`'s

```reason
| FunNoEnv(dp, d3) when mode == `Substitution => …step…
| FunNoEnv(_) => Indet          // environment mode: silently final
```

and the application is final-but-stuck forever. The issue has the full mechanism and why it presents nondeterministically in a live session; the short version is that `Transition`'s `Closure` rule evaluates subterms with `~in_closure`, which correctly omits the `Closure` wrapper for a function value nested under one — but a cache entry is keyed by id alone and is replayed at top level, where that enclosing `Closure` is gone.

The fix is a `carries_env` guard: don't reuse a value that carries no environment of its own.

## Testing

The bug is a good example of a class of defect our evaluator tests structurally could not reach, so the test is worth a look.

**Why a normal evaluator test can't see it.** Reuse is keyed on ids, so the cached ids have to survive from one program into the next. That only happens when the *same document* is edited in place. Two separate parses of the same text mint disjoint ids, so nothing is reused and nothing is exercised. Any reuse bug of this shape is invisible to a test that calls `Evaluator.evaluate` on parsed terms, however the terms are built.

**The test runs the editor's real update loop**, one frame of what `ScratchMode` does:

```reason
CellEditor.Update.update(~settings, MainEditor(Perform(action)), model).model
|> CellEditor.Update.calculate(
     ~settings=settings.core, ~is_edited=true, ~queue_worker=None, ~stitch=x => x)
```

With `~queue_worker=None`, `EvalResult.Update.calculate` builds the request itself, evaluates it through `WorkerServer.evaluate_sync`, and stores `incr_eval` in the model. So request construction, the choice of `EvalInfo.of_info_map`, and the threading of `prev` across keystrokes are all **covered** rather than restated by the test, and evaluation happens after every keystroke because that is what the editor does. Settings come from `Settings.Model.init`, the app's own defaults, rather than a hand-built `CoreSettings`.

That property is the point. An earlier version of this test built the request itself, and the first version of it reached for `EvalInfo.of_targets` — which leaves `reuse_check`'s `EvalInfo.find_opt` empty, so **incremental reuse never fires and the test passes no matter what `reuse_check` does**. A harness that restates the web stack can silently stop testing the thing it was written for; one that calls into it cannot. Worth knowing for any future evaluator harness.

What's left in the test file is fixture setup (`Parser.to_zipper` into a `CellEditor.Model.t`), a two-line action wrapper, and reading the value out of `model.result`.

**Determinism.** In a live session `prev` is a function of the whole editing history, so the same final text reproduces or not depending on how it was reached. The `test` block in the fixture pins that ingredient down so the regression test doesn't depend on history — see the comment above it.

It lives in `test/Test_CellEditor.re`, since `CellEditor` is the module it drives.

## Verification

- The new test fails on `dev` and passes with the guard.
- 460 `Evaluator` tests pass, including all incremental-reuse tests.
- `make` clean, no new warnings.
- Also confirmed end-to-end in the browser on the branch where this was found.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`| FunNoEnv(_) => Indet` fails silently — no error, no warning, just an application that stops reducing. A `DynamicErrorHole` there would have made this a much faster diagnosis. Noted on #2462.
