title: Roundtrip: Canonical completion + Shard/Lexeme Provenance
body:
Closes #2381
Closes #1792
Closes #2296
Subsumes #2079
References #2373 (known-outstanding)

## Goal: round-tripping

This PR makes every editor-reachable state round-trip: the buffer's segment parses to a term, and printing that term (segment-to-segment, via ExpToSegment) reproduces the original (tile ids, labels, shards, secondary) up to a small quotient described below. This is supported by property-based testing. Previously many states didn't survive the trip: incomplete tiles were dumped or dropped, quotes around labels and leading + in sum types disappeared, literal spellings normalized (007 -> 7, 4.0 -> 4.), unknown infix operators created multiholes which lost the operator string, etc.

This enables transforms on terms (eg refactorings, agent edits) while perserving all previously ephemeral editor state. The stacked refactorings PR is the first consumer.

The mechanism has two halves: canonical completion turns every incomplete segment into a well-formed one deterministically, and a small amount of lexical provenance recorded on terms lets the segment printer reconstruct exactly what the user had typed.

## Canonical completion

This assigns a canonical completion to every incomplete segment. Unlike the previous dump logic, canonical completions do not depend on caret position. However, ergonomic completions can't depend simply on
term structure: when inserting a new form, e.g. a let expression above existing code, term structure alone is ambiguous as to whether the new code wraps the code below or sits purely above it. The caret-based heuristic used previously is (a) only useful for incomplete forms in the caret segment, and (b) necessitates either re-completing on caret movement (expensive and potentially confusing) or a hidden history dependence (confusing).

The new heuristic is based on partitioning, meaning which following content an incomplete form absorbs. This is decided by indentation: after a linebreak, content at same-or-lesser indentation than the incomplete tile's line ends the partition. This subsumes the old, somewhat ugly "reset after a blank line" heuristic and is the intent-based discrimination discussed next.

Where the missing delimiters go — placement follows an evidence hierarchy (details in plans/completion-heuristics.md): a leftover prefix token (`i` for a deleted `in`, `-` for `->`) or the deletion's own junction debris pins the delimiter exactly where it was; only evidence-free states fall back to the structural defaults below. The engine completes ONE tile per pass (strongest evidence first, weak ties innermost-first) and recurses on the materialized result, so the suggestion set is a replay script: applying everything shown reproduces the computed result by construction, and jointly-broken forms (delete a case's `end` AND its let's `in`) restore compatibly.
- Missing closers are appended at the end of their partition, stopping before a span-final trailing operator when that strictly reduces synthesized holes (`test 1 == 1 end;` restores with the `end` before the `;`). A single-line form's closer glues back over a trailing linebreak (`let x = 1` + blank line + `2` takes its `in` on the definition line); a multiline form keeps its closer on its own line (a broken multiline case-def restores `end in` exactly where it was).
- Missing openers are placed at the start of their closer's left-operand span in the partition skel — the maximal span the completed form can absorb without crossing enclosing structure — bounded by line-walls: a deleted mid-program `let`/`if`/`case` head stays on its own line instead of absorbing the definitions above. So let a = 1,2] completes to let a = [1,2] in ?, not by hoisting [ above the let. Same-position ties open the later closer outermost: 1) + 2) -> ((1) + 2). Opener spans are also clamped by slot sort: a restored head lands at the nearest span that fits its interior slot (the second `let` of `let a = 1 in let b = 2 in b`, deleted inline, restores at `b` — a complete let can't be a pattern), while Exp-slot wrappers like a deleted `(` keep the maximal wrap.
- Missing middle delimiters (let x in 2, if true else 2; targeted put-down can strand an interior delimiter in the backpack) can't be appended like the others, because reassembly requires shard order. The tile is instead completed in place: each original child stays in the slot opened by its original left shard, and newly created slots get a hole, so let x in 2 completes to let x = ? in 2. The synthesized grout ids derive deterministically from surrounding tile ids, so completion is stable across recomputation.

## Indentation now user-owned

A non-obvious part of this design is that the indentation heuristic requires making indentation user-owned. This isn't
essential for round-tripping itself, but it's what makes canonical completion ergonomic, as well as resolveing a problem of its own.

Indentation around incomplete code has the same wrapping-uncertainty as completion, and on dev it leads to indentation thrashing: typing on one line causes lines below to indent and unindent repeatedly. So the row-indentation system is removed in favor of 'traditional' indentation: indentation is now simply regular whitespace (secondary), owned by the user.

Like conventional editors, we don't re-indent everything on every edit. Pressing enter inserts indentation after the new linebreak only, using the same indentation logic as before, so left-to-right entry gets the indentation you expect and nothing below the caret moves. **Cmd+S formats per a 4-level setting (none / indent / spaces / breaks; default respaces + re-indents); Cmd+Shift+S always pretty-prints.**

There is a nut menu setting, on by default, for limited auto-identation: Completing a delimiter re-indents the lines it affects. Settled (roughly: not containing incomplete tiles) regions get exact re-indentation; unsettled ones a uniform shift.

The presence of user-owned indentation is what allows intent-based discrimination: the completion only absorbs following lines if they are indented relative to the incomplete form's line. The user can indent/dedent to get the behavior they want, but in practice they don't have to, because the enter-inserted indentation suffices for the completion to do what you expect during left-to-right entry, whether writing new code or code above existing code.

The general principle is to move all history sensitivity into secondary, and all system history-dependence into auto-formatting behavior. The user has full control over secondary, so none of this is fundamentally hidden or out of their control. When the code is complete, autoformat erases any trace of historical dependence; it exists purely during incomplete states.

## What round-tripping adds data-structure-wise

Two new fields on the IdTag annotation:
- incomplete: list((Id.t, list(int))): for each canonically completed tile, which shards the user actually typed. The
printer strips synthesized shards on the way back out, so incomplete tiles survive the trip; MakeTerm threads the same masks so statics sees the completed form.
- lexeme: option(string): surface spellings the term normalizes, e.g. 007, 1e3, implicit vs ? vs ?? hole flavor, quoted labels, unknown infix operators (which now elaborate as stuck applications rather than evaluating to their last operand as multi-holes do).

Copy semantics are documented on the type: id-bearing fields drop on copy, value-meaning fields persist.

All other roundtrip gaps filled exploit existing structure rather than new fields. A representative trick: whether a sum type had a leading + is encoded by collected id count, as a leading-plus parse absorbs the separator ids, yielding n ids for n variants, while a bare binary sum carries only the n-1 separators; evaluator-built sums (single id) print bare, which reparses to the same type. Similarly, middle-completion hole ids derive from the tile id instead of being stored.

## Preserved property + fuzzing

The roundtrip property is enforced by a QCheck fuzzer driving Perform.go with random insert/move/destruct sequences from the empty buffer, sampling the actual editor-reachable domain, which parser based generators would undersample (rule tiles only form inside cases; deleted openers, standalone |/=> tokens, some grout cases are edit-reachable only). Also added a corpus and shrunk-counterexample regression suites.

What's compared: canonical completion yields a deeply complete segment whose parse prints back with identical text and piece sequence (tile ids, labels, shards, secondary), modulo a canonical quotient (grout (ephemeral by design), and mold sorts). Spelling, shapes, and precedences compare strictly.

Measured on the fuzzer (5 seeds, 290 states): the grout quotient earns its keep on placement, not ids — grout lands where the parsed term doesn't reproduce it in ~23% of reachable states (dangling boundary grout, stray grout glommed through MakeTerm), while ids agree whenever placement does. (The 4 id-only exceptions traced to the printer minting fresh ids on multihole id shortfalls; padding is now derived, so printing is a pure function of the term.)

The decision to quotient grout ids & sorts is pragmatic; there are currently a number of edge cases, some of which have been addressed, but i think the move it towards making both of these dervied; this is already underway for grout on the virtual-grout branch. If we don't decided to make these derived, we could add more annotations to avoid the need to quotient. In any case you can currently roptionally un the fuzzer with the quotient disabled enumerates to exactly the disagreement states derivation or annotation must handle.

An example of an outstanding sort issue: type : then ]. The editor molds the orphan ] at Typ — the caret sits on the typ side of the :. but canonical completion places the missing [ at the start, reading the state as [? : ?] (an Exp list whose element is the ascription, not ? : [?]), so the reprint derives the ] at Exp. 

Other known generator limitations: it fuzzes single-char insertion, char-wise movement, and backspace (so no selections, backpack pick-up/put-down, or copy/paste) and excludes projectors (follow-up work).

## Later additions (building on the roundtrip)

- **Completion heuristics**: missing delimiters drop into the concave junction their deletion left when shape + sort + uniqueness agree (`let x 1 in 2` -> `let x = 1 in 2`; deleted `else`/`in`/case-bars restore in place); `fun x` over a let-body clips the arrow at the sort frontier instead of absorbing the let into the pattern; a backspaced delimiter's leftover prefix token (`i` for `in`) is completed in place, recorded as a partially-typed shard (`{present, prefixes}` mask) so the roundtrip still closes exactly; leading witnesses restore deleted form heads from their remnants (`le` -> `let`, mid-program); sort-aware symbolic witnesses complete `-` -> `->` and `=` -> `=>`; broken cases repair as one case (wrap/opener arbitration + rule walls), and rules are treated as case-content throughout — mid-entry `case foo |` keeps its `end` after the growing rule.
- **Scoreboard instruments** (Test_CompletionScoreboard, pinned): deletion-inverse restoration over a corpus — full-deletion, last-char-prefix, joint pair-deletion (restoration + delimiter-completeness), and acceptance-stability (applying one suggestion must not move the rest; 96/104 stable, shifts only on known jointly-interacting states). Every remaining miss is a documented accepted-inherent (e.g. `f(3 + f(4)` is byte-identical to a freshly typed wide paren).
- **Quiver chips**: completion suggestions render as interline signposts at their exact placements — a bubble on the line boundary with a ghost-caret pole pinning the insertion column — replacing the old end-of-line boxes. Pins follow the caret through semantically-free whitespace; typed prefixes render cut-out; colorways distinguish tab-territory (pale) from other-segment obligations (gold); at caret coincidence the real caret is authoritative and the chip's pole steps aside.
- **Discharge routes**: `ApplyCompletion(All | One(tile))` materializes the virtual completion into the buffer (caret preserved by id). Alt+M completes everything (replacing the old greedy Dump, now deleted); cmd/ctrl+click on a chip completes exactly that delimiter (pointer cursor while the modifier is held; unmodified clicks pass through to the editor); tab still puts down at the caret. Agent/composition flows materialize through the same engine.
- **TyDi delimiter suffixes**: the ghost suggestion survives on prefix states where completion consumed the token's statics entry (ci-free witness route), 1-char expectation-backed prefixes bypass the length gate (`-`/`=` get arrow completions), and suggestions come from the same witness recognition the engine uses — ghost and quiver agree by construction. Tab at `els` accepts to `else` instead of dropping a fresh delimiter after it.
- **Reassociation**: retyping a deleted keyword char mid-program re-pairs with its orphaned shards (rescan matches singletons only; the repair fallback now explodes remnants and tries the sibling scope); `deep_reassociate` is no longer a setting — reassociation is unconditional, and the harnesses run it (they previously silently didn't, hiding this bug class from every edit-derived test).
- **Formatting**: SpaceNormalize gains an opt-in canonicalize mode (mold-aware within-line respacing: `f (x)` -> `f(x)`, one space around infix ops, comments/linebreaks untouched) backing the new Spaces format level; format actions restore the caret via CaretPreserving (from #2231 — exact piece, else surviving predecessor, else ancestors). Printing is now a pure function of the term (pad_ids derives instead of minting).
- **Auto-reindent triggers**: paste re-indents the pasted lines (settled exact / unsettled uniform shift) and, like TyDi accept, destruct, and comment-toggle, runs the completion-triggered re-indent when a tile completes.
- **Indentation UX** (gated on a core setting, on by default): arrow movement skips leading whitespace (every line keeps one reachable position; clicks/selection stay char-exact); backspace at first-content inverts enter (indent + linebreak, one keystroke, one undo); Cmd+[/] indent/dedent lines from any position; Shift+Backspace dedents at the line-start boundary only.

## Removals

The backpack display is retired (the quiver is the completion display; the put-down mechanism and derived missing-shards machinery remain — internals renamed from "backpack" to missing_shards), along with `Dump`, the `deep_reassociate` setting, and the redundant NutMenu Docs toggle. Persisted settings blobs lose two fields, so browsers may see a one-time settings reset.

## Addendum

- A batch of fidelity fixes found by the fuzzer along the way, including the two closed issues above.
(cross-sort tiles in MakeTerm, crossed synthesized delimiters, adjacent-operator lexemes, typ-side incomplete forms, and more); #2373 remains outstanding.
- docs/segments.md documents the round-trip contract, the provenance fields, and the sort-quotient rationale with the example above.
- Possible future refinements, deferred: sort re-derivation as above; virtual grout (#2165) as the same derive-don't-store program applied to grout.

title: Modules II, part 3: abstract type members, sealing, path types
body:
Third of the stack, on top of #2494. A signature may declare `type T` with no definition; a module sealed by it must define `T`, but outside the module `T` is known only as the path `M.T`.

- **Syntax.** `type T` is a signature item (`SigTypeAbstract`) in the grammar, the tile forms (listed before the manifest form so that `type` typed in a signature expands to it), `MakeTerm`, the Menhir `sigItem` rule, the printers, equality, abbreviation and ExplainThis. In the editor, typing `=` after a bare `type T` upgrades the tile to `type T = …` (`Insert.upgrade_bare_sig_type`); there is no downgrade.
- **Sealing.** A module analyzed against `{ type T; let x : T }` must define `T` (a missing definition is a `ModuleMissingMembers`; a value named `T` does not count), and its members are checked against its own definition. `Typ.sig_sub` realizes an abstract member of the required signature by whatever the module provides; a manifest member is not satisfied by an abstract one. `Typ.meet` matches abstract members only with abstract members.
- **Path types.** An abstract member projected from a module path is the stuck normal form `M.T`, consistent with itself and `?` only. `Typ.path_sig` now returns the path along with the items; `weak_head_normalize`, `normalize` and `meet` stop at a stuck path. A module variable's type is strengthened (`Typ.strengthen`, at `Var`, the capitalized-constructor fallback and `Dot`), so `M.x : M.T` and `module N = M` shares `M.T`, while two modules sealed by the same signature have distinct types. Only a path can name an abstract type: projecting from any other expression, or through a signature alias, gives `?`. The cursor inspector reports `M.T` as an abstract type (`Message.PathAbstract`).
- **Dynamics.** Abstract members have no runtime content. Runtime sealing now ascribes each kept member to its closed type, so an abstract member casts to `?` (previously a bare `T` left stuck casts such as `0:T`).

Tests: eighteen `Statics.Modules` cases (sealing, path types, aliasing, distinct sealings, transparency, missing and kind mismatches, forward references), `Typ.SigPaths`, `Evaluator.Modules`, `Editing.SigAbstract` (bare form, `=` upgrade, Cmd+D), plus MakeTerm, Menhir, round-trip, TyDi and Equality cases. Slide section F (a `Counter` module) and `docs/modules.md` describe the design.

Known, planned for the next PR: `fun (m : { type T; let x : T }) -> m.x` currently types as `S -> m.T` with `m` escaping its scope; the generative `Typ.avoid` handles that.

## Known gaps

- **No sharing constraint.** There is no `with type` spelling, so a signature
  cannot be refined by fixing one member, and nothing says the equivalent of
  `SHOW with T = Int`. The workaround is a hand-written signature literal
  carrying a manifest member, which is verbose and easy to get wrong; the
  implicits part (#2508) documents it because resolution needs it often.
- **No opaque-versus-transparent ascription.** One colon seals, and a sealed
  module's type members can never be selected by an argument type, so a
  sealed implicit instance is unusable. That is documentation today rather
  than a language distinction; a second spelling that checks against a
  signature while keeping manifest types would remove the footgun.
- **Type members cannot take parameters.** The type-pattern grammar admits a
  bare name, so nothing abstracting over a type constructor is expressible:
  no collection, monad or functor signature. Value members may be
  polymorphic, so signatures in the style of show, equality and monoid are
  unaffected.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (3600 tests).

## Follow-up commits

- **Report a missing member once, and let signatures name sibling members.** The synthetic `x : T` expectation checked inside a module body no longer shares ids with the signature's type nodes, and is skipped when it mentions a name the module does not define, so a missing `type T` is reported only on the module. Signature items can now see earlier value and module members, so `{ module Inner : { type T }; let y : Inner.T }` is well-formed; in subtyping a sibling is bound to the type the module provides.
- **The Modules slide is split here** rather than in part 4: sections E and F move to `module-signatures.hz`, because statics recursion depth grows with the `let` chain and the combined slide was at the JavaScript stack limit (jsoo overflows node's default stack at roughly 100 nested lets).
- **An abstract member cannot be named through a signature alias.** `type S = { type T; … } in let y : S.T = …` used to type `S.T` as `?`, so any value passed and the inspector called `?` an abstract type. The alias names no module, so there is no particular `T` to name: it is now an error on the label (`TypAbstractMemberOfSignature`), with the dot explaining that a module `M` of the signature names it as `M.T`; TyDi no longer suggests such members. Manifest members through an alias, and abstract members through a module path, are unchanged. A type path rooted at a base type name (`Nat.T`) now says the name is a base type, not a module. Slide item 36a.

title: Modules II, part 1: first-class signature types and module values
body:
First of a stack of three (a fourth, module-typed function parameters and returns, follows). This one replaces the labeled-tuple gloss described in `docs/modules.md` with real module statics and dynamics; the next two add width subtyping and abstract type members on top.

## Statics

- `Sig` is a distinct, first-class type. `Typ.desugar_sig` is gone and a signature is inconsistent with a labeled tuple type in both directions. Signatures are dependent records: `free_vars`, `subst`, `normalize` and `meet` treat type members as sequential binders, and `meet` requires the same member names (exact; width arrives in the next PR). `Sig.re` exposes the member view (`Val`, `TypeManifest`).
- A module synthesizes its signature in source order (`ModuleHelpers.module_sig_type`). Against an annotated signature, manifest type members are checked (`ModuleTypeMemberMismatch` on the `type` item) and substituted into member expectations; missing members mark the module (`ModuleMissingMembers`).
- `M.T` resolves through the module variable's signature (`Typ.path_sig`, including `M.P.T`, module aliasing and signature aliases). The `TVarEntry` injection in the `Let` case is removed. `Dot` projects signature members.
- `module M : S` is a signature item too (`SigModule`), so capitalized sub-modules can be declared inline. Module items report the member they declare in the cursor inspector.

## Dynamics

- Modules evaluate as modules. `Transition.re` steps `Module(items)` item by item with sequential scoping; an evaluated binding becomes the dynamics-only item `ModVal(x, v)`, and a module of `ModVal`s is a value. `Dot` reads bindings by name; ascribing a module value to a signature seals it. New `EvalCtx.ModuleItem` / `ModuleVal` contexts.
- Statics still lowers a module body to a `Let`/`TyAlias` chain for type checking (reusing the `Let` and pattern machinery); elaboration refolds the checked chain back into a `Module`.

## Also

TyDi qualified completions read signature members; the cursor inspector and `ErrorPrint` render the new marks; `docs/modules.md` and the Modules doc slide are rewritten; tests migrated (module types are signatures, module values are modules). One skipped test pins a known gap: `{ let ? : ? }` should eventually match any member once the hole is filled.

## Known gaps

Module structure, roughly by how much each blocks real programs. None is a
regression; they are what this construct does not reach yet.

- **Constructors declared inside a module are not members of it** (#2243).
  Qualified access fails and the bare name leaks into the enclosing scope, so
  two modules declaring the same constructor make that name unusable. This
  breaks the ordinary idiom of a type and its operations in one module.
- **Signature items accept arbitrary patterns and then bind nothing** (#2242).
  A tuple-pattern member is accepted, declares no members, and member access
  on the binder then reports that the module has none.
- **No `include` and no `open`** (#2260, #2261). Reusing a signature or
  bringing members into scope is copy-paste, which makes larger signatures
  repetitive.
- **No module destructuring in patterns.** Only a name, optionally
  signature-annotated, can bind a module; there is no way to pull several
  members out at once.
- **No mutually recursive modules**, and modules are values inside one
  program rather than compilation units, so there is no import story.
- **Module equality is not rejected statically**, only incomparable at
  runtime.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green · no push before manual browser testing was the plan, so please treat this as reviewed-by-tests only.

## Follow-up commits

- **Module-aware projection errors, one error per differing type member.** `m.y` with no member `y` now marks the label (`ModuleMemberNotFound`, which also says when `y` is a type member used as a value) and gives the dot only a message, the design the type-level `M.Fake` already had. `M.T` with no type member `T`, a missing sub-module in `M.P.T`, and a value used as the root of a type path get module-aware marks and wording; the dot marks that said "tuple" say "module or tuple". A manifest type member that differs from the signature is reported once, on its `type` item: members are checked against the module's own definition. Slide items 11a to 11d show the messages.
- **The function shorthand binds a member.** `let f(x) = ...` in a module body exported `x` rather than `f` (#2467, #2295): binders were read with `Pat.bound_vars`, which treats an applied pattern as a constructor application. The lowering reads a let item's binder through `FunctionSugar.binder` and annotates a shorthand at its name with the type its signature expects; the `Let` case of statics then desugars it exactly as it does a top-level shorthand.

Closes #2467. Closes #2295.

title: Modules II, part 2: width subtyping at analysis positions
body:
Second of the stack, on top of #2493. Where an expression is analyzed against a signature, the module may have more members than the signature declares; the extra members are sealed away.

## Motivation

### What width subtyping is for

Part 1 made modules first-class values whose types are signatures, but with an *exact* relation between them: `{ let x = 1; let y = 2 }` had type `{ let x : Int; let y : Int }` and nothing else. That makes a signature a description of one module rather than an interface, and it rules out the things modules exist for:

- **Interfaces.** `let greet = fun (m : { let name : String }) -> "hello " ++ m.name` should accept any module that has a `name`. Without width, only a module with exactly one member fits, so every caller has to build a fresh module of the right shape.
- **Information hiding.** `module Stack : { let empty : …; let push : …; let top : … } = { let default = 0; … }` should be allowed to keep helpers like `default` private. Without width, a signature can never omit anything, so nothing can be hidden.
- **Evolution.** Adding a member to a module should not break code written against its signature.

Width subtyping gives all three: a module fits a signature that declares a subset of its members. The members the signature omits are *sealed away*: the binder's type is the signature as written, `m.y` on a member the signature omits is an error, and at runtime the module value keeps only the signature's members (`Ascriptions.re`). Slide section E walks through each case.

### Where it applies

Only at **analysis positions**: places where the program states the type an expression must have.

| Position | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `let` / `module` annotation | `module M : { let x : Int } = { let x = 1; let y = 2 }` |
| Ascription | `({ let x = 1; let y = 2 } : { let x : Int })` |
| Function argument | `greet({ let name = "Alice"; let age = 30 })`, `greet(Alice)` |
| Annotated pattern | `fun (m : { let x : Int }) -> …` binds `m` at the narrower type |
| Depth, through members | `{ module Db : { let host : String } }` accepts a `Db` that also has `port` |
| Function domains, contravariantly | a `{ let x : Int } -> Int` fits where a `{ let x : Int; let y : Int } -> Int` is required |

The check is `Typ.ana_meet(ctx, ~ana, ~syn)`: exact `Typ.meet` first, and only if that fails a directional check, `Typ.sig_sub`, which walks the *required* signature's members and asks the *provided* one for each. Its result is the required type, which is what seals the binder. Two invariants hold: `meet(a, b) ≠ None ⇒ ana_meet(~ana=a, ~syn=b) ≠ None`, and `ana_meet = meet` whenever the required type is not a signature or a function type (`Typ.AnaMeet` tests both).

### What it deliberately does not do, and why

- **Consistency stays exact.** `Typ.meet` is unchanged, so `if b then { let x = 1 } else { let x = 1; let y = 2 }` is an error, as are `case` arms, list elements and the operands of `==` with different member sets. The wider branch must be ascribed: `else ({ let x = 1; let y = 2 } : { let x : Int })`. Three reasons. First, `meet` is Hazel's consistency relation in the sense of Siek and Taha (2006): symmetric, with `?` as the top of a lattice, and used as a lattice operation for joins, for incremental-evaluation reuse and for equality. A directional rule inside it would break symmetry and the idempotence the rest of the system assumes. Second, a join of signatures *could* be defined (the members they share), but then a branch would silently lose members with no ascription anywhere to point at, and the runtime would have to seal both branches to a type nobody wrote. Keeping subsumption at analysis positions means every sealing is visible in the source. Third, conservatism against the two reference implementations: the labeled-tuple gloss on `dev` and the 2023 `haz3l-module` branch both compared signatures by exact member lists, so this PR widens exactly one dimension, in exactly the positions ML does (see below), and nothing else changes type.
- **No width for tuples.** `(x=1, y=2) : (x=Int)` remains an error. Labeled tuples are positional products with labels, not interfaces; `Prod` and `Sig` are distinct types in part 1 and stay that way.
- **No subtyping under other constructors.** Only signatures (depth through members) and function types (contravariant domain, covariant codomain) get structural rules; `[wide] : [narrow]` is not accepted. Lists and products can be widened later if a use appears; nothing in the design blocks it.
- **Value members must match, not generalize.** A member's type is checked with `ana_meet` against the declared type; there is no instantiation of a more general scheme, since Hazel's polymorphism is explicit.
- **Sealing is static first.** A module that reaches a narrower type through `?` keeps its extra members at runtime; that is unobservable because statics forbids accessing them, and an ascription seals whenever one is present.

### Comparison with OCaml modules and functors

OCaml's signature matching is also structural and width-permissive: `module M : S = struct … end` accepts a structure with more components than `S` declares and hides the rest, and a functor application `F(M)` checks `M` against the parameter signature the same way (Leroy 1994). Matching happens at exactly the places this PR calls analysis positions: ascriptions and functor parameters. Elsewhere OCaml has no subtyping between module types either. First-class modules are packed at an explicit signature, `(module M : S)`, and two package types unify only when their module types are equal, so `if b then (module A : S1) else (module B : S2)` is rejected unless `S1` and `S2` coincide, the same boundary as the exact `meet` here. The correspondence is deliberate: a Hazel function over a module, `fun (m : S) -> …`, is a functor whose parameter is matched by width at each application, and an ascription `(m : S)` plays the role of `(module M : S)`.

Two places differ. OCaml functors are applicative by default (`F(M).t` is one type across applications to the same path) and generative only with a `()` parameter; Hazel's module-returning functions are generative per call (part 4), which is simpler and needs no path equivalence between applications in a gradual setting. And OCaml expresses sharing with `with type t = …` constraints; Hazel does it with manifest members and path types (`m.T`, part 3), which is closer to Leroy's manifest types and strengthening than to `with`.

### References

- Siek and Taha, *Gradual Typing for Functional Languages*, Scheme Workshop 2006: the consistency relation, symmetric and non-transitive, that `Typ.meet` implements.
- Siek and Taha, *Gradual Typing for Objects*, ECOOP 2007: consistent-subtyping, width subtyping on object types, and why subtyping and consistency must be composed as `S <: T' ~ T` rather than taken transitively through `?`. `ana_meet` is such a check confined to analysis positions.
- Garcia, Clark and Tanter, *Abstracting Gradual Typing*, POPL 2016: the general recipe for deriving a consistent subtyping relation from a static one.
- Cardelli, *A Semantics of Multiple Inheritance*, 1984/1988: width and depth subtyping on records.
- Leroy, *Manifest Types, Modules, and Separate Compilation*, POPL 1994, and *Applicative Functors and Fully Transparent Higher-Order Modules*, POPL 1995: signature matching, manifest versus abstract types, strengthening, applicative functors.
- Rossberg, Russo and Dreyer, *F-ing Modules*, JFP 2014: elaboration of ML modules into System F with subtyping at signature matching; the lowering of module bodies to `let` chains in part 1 is in this spirit.
- Rossberg, *1ML: Core and Modules United*, JFP 2018: modules as first-class values with subtyping at ascription, the closest published design to this stack.

## What changed

- `Typ.ana_meet` / `Typ.sig_sub`: at analysis positions a signature fits a signature declaring a subset of its members (the wider one's type members are opened under fresh names), value members may themselves be wider, and functions are contravariant in their domain. Exact `meet` is tried first and remains the consistency relation for joins, `if` branches, equality and `is_consistent`.
- `StaticsBase.fixed_typ` / `expectation_mismatch_mark` / `syn_ana_ok_common` route through `ana_meet`, with `_pat` variants that swap the required and provided roles for pattern checks. Returning the expected type is what seals a binder: `m.y` on a module sealed to `{ let x : Int }` is a `LabelNotFound`.
- `ModuleExtraMembers` (added in the previous PR) is retired; hole-named signature members no longer cause an error.
- Dynamics: the last binding step yields the module value marked final, so evaluated bindings are never re-traversed (re-traversal double-sampled probed literals). Runtime sealing keeps the signature's members in signature order.
- Incremental evaluation: a binding's ascription type is part of its reuse provenance (`Ascribed(Typ.t)`). Without it, editing a `module M : S = ...` signature let dependents of `M` reuse values computed under the old signature.

Tests cover width in `let` / ascription / `module` / function-argument / bound-variable / nested positions, contravariance, the exact-join boundary, `Typ.AnaMeet`, runtime sealing, probes and the incremental-eval regression. Slide section E shows structural interfaces, hidden helpers, depth, contravariance and the join boundary.

## Known gap

Analysis-position subtyping has no list arm. A list of unsealed modules is
rejected against a list of signatures even though each element is checked and
sealed on its own, and both the element error and the list error are reported;
ascribing each element is the workaround. This looks like a one-arm addition
next to the signature, arrow and tuple cases.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green.

title: Incremental eval leaves a binding unsubstituted when evaluation gets stuck after an edited literal
body:
## Summary

The QCheck property **"Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit"** (`test/evaluator/Test_Evaluator_Properties.re:307`, `~count=2000`) fails for some seeds. It presents as a flake, but it isn't: given a program of the right shape it fails **every time**. Only whether QCheck generates that shape is random.

Minimal repro, no seed needed:

```hazel
{ let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }
```

Edit the `4` to `5` (which is what the property does — a type-preserving `+1` on an int literal), then evaluate the edited program two ways:

| | result |
|---|---|
| fresh (no `prev`) | `let true = A in (x=(()))` |
| incremental (`prev` = original's `incr_eval`) | `let true = A in (x=x)` |

Both get stuck on the failing pattern match `let true = A`, as expected. The disagreement is in the residual environment: **fresh has substituted `x`'s value, incremental has left `x` as a variable.** `Equality.semantic.exp` then reports them unequal, which is what fails the property.

## Required ingredients

Removing or reordering any of these makes it pass, which should localize it:

- **A named binding before the literal.** `let x = ()` fails; `let _ = ()` passes — the name has to survive into the residual.
- **The literal bound to `_`.** `let _ = 4` fails; `let y = 4` passes.
- **Evaluation must get stuck *after* the literal.** `{ let true = A; let _ = 4 }` (stuck first) passes.
- **Stuck via a pattern-match failure, not an unbound variable.** `let true = q` passes; `let true = A`, `let true = ()`, `let false = A`, `let 7 = A` all fail.

Irrelevant: the literal's value (`0` and `4` both fail), and the number of preceding bindings — `{ let x = (); let z = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }` fails with `(x=x, z=z)` against `(x=(()), z=(()))`, so every named binding is affected, not just the first.

## Seeds

`QCHECK_SEED=3` and `QCHECK_SEED=468045375` both reproduce via the property itself; `QCHECK_SEED=1` and `2` pass. Seed 3 shrinks to

```
(0, { let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A; type y = y; type ? = Bool; type x = Void })
```

and the three trailing type aliases are incidental — the minimal case above is what's left after removing them.

## Why this matters now

This is a **second** flaky-looking property, distinct from #2128 ("Evaluator and stepper are consistent"). #2422 makes the test runner propagate a real exit status, so from that point a tripped property **blocks** rather than merely annotating a green run. With `~count=2000` and no fixed seed, both will start failing PRs intermittently.

Two things worth deciding alongside a fix: whether the residual should substitute (fresh's behaviour looks right, but that's a call for whoever owns incremental eval), and whether these properties should carry a fixed seed in CI with randomized seeds in a periodic run, so a real regression is distinguishable from a newly-unlucky draw.

## Reproducing without QCheck

The helpers the property uses are all top-level in `Test_Evaluator_Properties.re` (`collect_int_lits`, `replace_int_lit_by_id`, `statics_and_elab`, `eval_limited`), so the case above can be driven directly from parsed text — which is how it was minimized, and probably how it should be pinned as a regression test once fixed.

title: Probes IV
body:
Probes features and fixes from the study branch. Subsumes #2321 and #2325 (now closed).

Closes #2067
Closes #2323
Closes #2276
Closes #2217

## Features

- **Drawer mode.** Expand a probe's sample into a multi-line, pretty-printed block below the code line (`Cmd/Ctrl+↓` open / `Cmd/Ctrl+↑` close, or the row's chevron; Esc exits). Per-probe state, capped at 15 rows (scrolls beyond). Built on a new `below` projector view slot reserving rows via `Tab(n)`.
- **Enhanced Auto-probe** Auto-probe now probes top-level expressions as well ad defiitions. Auto-probe now has an `All` mode. Modes are `Off | Caret | All` (was on/off). _Caret_ probes the top-level definition under the cursor; _All_ probes the whole program, one probe per source row (a single root multiprobe). `Cmd/Ctrl+P` cycles Off↔All; the sidebar's segmented control also reaches Caret.
- **"Simple" color scheme (new default).** Two colors: focal-call green vs. off-focus washed out green. replacing the old Hybrid default. Use the toggle in the sidebar to access the old default.

## Fixes (pre-existing behavior)

- **Probe samples no longer stale until the next edit:** Placing a probe (or autoprobe) showed the ∅ indicator until the next edit, because the statics debounce left `probe_targets` stale and `IncrEval.reuse_check` reused a sampleless slice. Now a probe-id change forces a full statics refresh. (Also makes auto-probe work in exercise mode.)
- **Step-into for indirect calls.** Extends the existing step-into to higher-order calls, partial applications, and `let f x = …` sugar, by carrying a resolved call frame (`fn_def_id`) through evaluator state into each sample.
- **More stable Sample-ids to prevent collisions on deep recursion** — fixes double-indication, twin resize handles, and broken scroll anchors via collision-resistant ids.
- **Accurate Tab projector/refractor decoration offset** — Code/decoration row desync from out-of-order deferred-linebreak counting is fixed.
- **Projector action index crash** — a stale render-time index now drops the action instead of raising.
- Smaller: duplicate manual-refractor entry (assoc-list vs map disagreement), stuck pending probe cursor, a sibling-cleanup toggle that re-added forever, and pointer/drag guards.

## Modifications / polish

- **Sample-count indicator moved** from an overlay circle on the projector to an inline badge at the start of the samples row (hidden for a single sample).
- **Sample dropdown now uses right-/alt-click.** The sample dropdown (which shows environment variables and pin/step options) opens on right-click or alt-click (was hover-only), with click-outside / scroll dismissal. Hover activation proved to hyperactive.
- **Function-sugar probing.** Putting a multi-probe on `let f(args) = body` now probes the arguments on the header line, not just the body.
- **Sample-focus navigation now scrolls horizontally:** When using ←/→ move the focused sample it should scroll-follow it into view; this previously only worked vertically.
- Indeterminant samples e.g. holes no longer colored differently than value samples; this proved confusing to multiple people.
- Removed the dashed connector line between probes and samples; added visual noise doesn't pay for itself.
- Sidebar quick-reference updated for new interactions (alt-click for env, right-click for pin/step, an expand-probe row).
- Focus bar: "Clear all" also turns auto-probe off; the editor caret stays visible after a focus-bar / sidebar jump.
- Scroll stability for drawer refractors: drawer-height changes above the caret are prevented from shifting it via scroll trigger.
- Tuple pretty-printing breaks symmetrically
- The test pass/fail badge no longer floats above probe sample menu.

## Performance

- Viewport culling now re-enabled, but only for auto-probe All mode (infra already existed on dev but was inert): off-screen probe views are culled in the single-editor modes (Scratch / Documentation / Tutorial); Exercises stays unculled.
- Cull-before-build for probe views, memoized multi-probe expansion + placeholder calcs, and phys-equality gating on rebuilds.

## Late additions: cards + rich-view UX (2026-08-22)

- Cherry-picks Alexander's card RichProbe renderer (authorship preserved) (from `card-rich-probe`), forward-ported to this branch's registry API (`empty`, `drawer_rows`), with card/hand shape-matching intact.
- Rich views render **inside** the sample chip (green backing, inert content) rather than replacing the row — the chip keeps the dropdown (Hide), sample capture, dbl-click, and resize. The anchored modal is retired: small rich views (≤4 rows) embed in the row; taller ones auto-open the drawer on activation. Many mode shows one card/fan per sample.
- **Rich Views** toggle in the probes sidebar (default on): probes auto-render the first applicable renderer when it fits; double-click flips an individual probe back to text. Tables remain opt-in.
- Empty hands render a card-footprint silhouette (dotted outline, ∅) instead of nothing.
- Offside **stagger**: an after-display pass floors each display at the end of every code line it spans and first-fits it among displays from rows above, so multi-row content (card fans) overlaps neither program text nor other probes.

Fumola livelits: running an incremental Fumola runtime from Hazel
body:
An experimental integration between Hazel and **Fumola**, a language whose execution model uses Adapton / demanded computation graphs, so that editing and re-running a program can reuse prior computation rather than starting over.

**Try it:** `hazel.org/build/fumola-livelit-mvp`, or `make && make serve`. No setup — the Fumola runtime is fetched from its published build. Type `^fumola_thunk` or `^fumola_editor` then space.

**Depends on** [Adapton/fumola#45](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/pull/45) and [#46](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/pull/46), both merged. Nothing binary is tracked here.

# Purpose of the MVP

Hazel and Fumola are each exploring live, responsive evaluation, and each relates itself to spreadsheets. Hazel's livelits are one such semantics; Fumola's demanded computation graph, where editing a program repairs prior computation rather than redoing it, is another.

This branch puts the second one *inside* the first: a Fumola runtime becomes something a Hazel program can hold and name, so two live evaluation models sit in one document, side by side, where they can be compared and composed.

Two livelits are the ways of reaching across. A **thunk** livelit holds a program whose value you are editing: it is wrapped in a named thunk, so re-forcing that name on each edit is what lets Fumola repair rather than recompute. An **editor** livelit holds a program run at the top level, for setting things up and for the operations a thunk cannot host — writing cells that thunks will read, making bindings that outlive the program, and reaching Adapton's own introspection.

**Instance ids are what keep Fumolas apart.** An id names a runtime, so a document can hold several independent ones, and livelits sharing an id share a store, a set of bindings and a demanded computation graph. Isolation and communication are both just a question of which id you write.

That framing is what makes the rest of this interesting. Every livelit shipped today is self-contained: `^slider`'s model *is* its value. These are the first whose model holds a **name for state that lives outside Hazel**, so the interesting question is not the widget but what it means for a Hazel value to denote something a foreign runtime owns.

A livelit's model names an entry of an external store

```text
Σ : FumolaInstanceId -> FumolaRuntimeState
```

held by the Fumola wasm module and reached through the `window.fumola` shim. The Fumola interpreter and its demanded computation graph are deliberately *not* serialized into the model; only the name is. Three consequences, each implemented explicitly rather than inherited:

- **Editing preserves the name**, so an edit re-evaluates against the same live runtime and state written in one edit is there in the next.
- **Expansion is an observation of Σ**, never a second source of truth in the model.
- **The runtime does the work.** There is no repair API in Fumola and none was needed: a thunk livelit wraps its program as ``force(`name := thunk { ... })``, and re-assigning that name and forcing it again is what makes the edit incremental. `:=` and `thunk` do the rest.

## Two livelits and a value

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `^fumola_thunk(instance, name, program)` | wraps its program in a named thunk; incremental across edits |
| `^fumola_editor(instance, program)` | evaluates at the top level; no reuse, but bindings outlive it |
| `FumolaPeek` | not a livelit — what a returned *pointer* becomes |

`^fumola_editor` is strictly more expressive: you can write the ``force(... := thunk { ... })`` yourself. What the thunk livelit adds is generating that wrapper with a distinct name. The editor is also the only way to reach what the wrapper forbids — `Adapton.reset()` clears the store the enclosing force is still inside, and `Adapton.peekForce` asserts there.

The **thunk name** is Fumola source for a symbol, parsed by Fumola itself, so ``​`myThunk``, `7` and ``​`a(`b)`` all work and Hazel needs to know about none of them. It is written rather than derived on purpose: a name taken from a Hazel id would start a *new* thunk whenever that id changed, quietly losing the history the thunk exists to keep.

Both name an instance, so **two livelits carrying the same id share one runtime**.

# Simple programs to try

Both livelits require an annotation — they only expand in checking mode, since the result's shape depends on the program.

**State surviving an edit.** Run this, then edit the program to just `get(1)`; it still reads `2`.

```
let n : Int = ^fumola_thunk(0, "`a", "1 := 2; get(1)") in n
```

**The worked example**, also in Documentation → Livelits → builtins. Three livelits over one runtime:

```
let x  : Int = ^fumola_thunk(0, "`t", "`x := 137 + 137; 137") in
let x_ : Int = ^fumola_editor(0, "pointer(`x)") in
let y  : Int = ^fumola_editor(0, "force(pointer(`t))") in
(x, x_, y)                    ->  (137, peek(`x)! = 274, 137)
```

The thunk writes a cell and returns 137. The first editor asks for a pointer to that cell, which arrives as a peek value showing **both the reference and what it holds**, typing as `Int` so the ascription is satisfied and evaluation continues through it. The second editor forces the thunk the *first livelit* made, by its name ``​`t`` — which is why explicit thunk names matter.

**Values that cross the boundary**, each verified against the runtime:

```
1 + 2                       ->  3
`counter := 41; get(`counter) + 1
                            ->  42
(1 := 10, 2 := 20)          ->  a pair of peek values
{x = 1; y = true}           ->  a Hazel record
peek(1)                     ->  Some(10)
peek(404)                   ->  None
`hello                      ->  "hello"
Gcd.gcd(12, 18)             ->  6     (module library, no import)
```

**Things needing `^fumola_editor`**, since they cannot run inside a thunk:

```
Adapton.reset()             ->  ()
Adapton.peekEvents()        ->  a list of records carrying events, spaces and times
```

**Always in scope:** `pointer(s)`, `get(s)`, `peek(s)`. They exist because Hazel string literals admit no escapes — `Token.is_string` permits at most two quote characters in a token — so a livelit's program can never contain a `"`, and every adapton primitive needs one. Note that `:=` coerces its left side into a pointer but `@` does not, so a cell is read back with `get(s)`.

**The module library is compiled into the runtime** and bound at the top level: `Adapton`, `List`, `LazyList`, `PureList`, `LevelTree`, `HashMap`, `Counters`, `RandomInput`, `MergeSort`, `Gcd`, `DelayedPut`. Anything else is reachable by path.

# Future work to explore

**Expansions are not typed.** Statics splices a livelit's expansion in as an already-elaborated term and never traverses it ([Statics.re](src/language/statics/Statics.re)). Three things follow: a livelit nested in an expansion is never expanded, so `FumolaPeek` cannot render as a widget; constructors inside an expansion are never resolved; and no annotation anywhere in the program can reach inside one. This branch works around it with type-directed expansion, but making expansions real syntax is the change that would dissolve several problems at once.

**Sum types across the boundary.** Fumola tags are structural and live in one flat namespace: `#Bar(3)` is a value whether or not anyone declared `Bar`. Hazel constructors are declaration-bound. So the boundary is lossy in the direction that matters — Fumola hands you a tag, Hazel needs a tag *plus* a home type. Expansion now resolves tags against the expected type, but round-tripping Hazel → Fumola → Hazel can still land in a different sum type.

**`Space` and `Time` both declare a `Symbol` constructor.** With an expected type it resolves correctly; without one it falls back to a context lookup that could pick either.

**Generative copy is not implemented.** A copied livelit inherits its original's instance id and shares its execution history. Doing it properly needs a projector identity that survives a model edit, which this branch does not establish.

**Instance lifetime across sessions.** A saved program naming instance 17 in a session with no `Σ(17)` realizes a fresh runtime, which then has no history. What *should* happen on reload is unsettled.

**The peek snapshot is load-bearing.** `FumolaPeek` carries a value that is sound only because it is regenerated on every expansion. Persisting one into a saved model would silently disagree with the runtime.

**Hazel has no parameterized types.** There is no type-level application, so `Option` is monomorphic with payload `?`. That is why `Option(SomeThing)` cannot be written, and why an option's payload type is lost on the way across.

**Pre-existing livelit issues found along the way**, two fixed here and two not — see the section below.

**Smaller ones.** Instance creation costs ~250ms and the wasm is 5.5MB, both from compiling in the module library; `Dot` symbols have no Fumola parser support; and `Adapton.peekForce` still fails inside a thunk, so introspection wants the editor.

# Pre-existing issues found along the way

Four problems in the livelit machinery with nothing to do with Fumola. Two were in the way and are fixed here; two are recorded but untouched.

**Fixed — clicking any livelit crashed.** `JsUtil.get_elem_by_id` ends in `assert(false)`, and `LivelitProj.focus_pointer` calls it on every pointer click — but the projector attaches its id only where `get_model` succeeds, so the `No livelit found` fallback asserted. Confirmed against deployed `dev`: `^slider` and `^emotion` crash on click there today.

**Fixed — a livelit with a text field could not be typed into.** Clicking the field focused it, then `Focus` refocused the projector's wrapper `<div>`, which has no `tabindex`; focusing an unfocusable element drops focus to `<body>`. So the field lost focus the instant it was clicked, and the only way to edit was to unproject the livelit. **This affects `^js` too.**

**Not fixed — livelits do not render in the Documentation slides.** All of them show `No livelit found`; verified on deployed `dev`. This is also why the two above went unnoticed: the widgets are invisible in the one place the docs point you at.

**Not fixed — livelits have no keyboard handoff.** `focusable.keyboard = None`, so arrow-key navigation into and out of one does not work. `TextAreaProj` is the model to follow: it puts the projector id directly on its textarea, which would subsume the focus fix above.

# Reviewer notes

- **The livelit interface changed**: `view` now takes `~id`, and `expand` takes `~id`, `~ana` and a `type_tools` record. Closures rather than a `Ctx.t`, because `Ctx` already depends on `LivelitCtx` and naming it there would be circular. The other three livelits ignore the new arguments.

This disables both and pins each bug deterministically instead. **It fixes neither bug** — #2128, #2372 and #2457 stay open.

| property | issue | reddened |
|---|---|---|
| `Evaluator and stepper are consistent` (case 5) | #2128, dup #2372 | a random local seed while preparing this PR |
| `Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit` (case 7) | #2457 | [33513972427](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33513972427), [33513747011](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33513747011), [33412342909](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33412342909) — three unrelated branches, each dying on case 7 alone |

Disabled the way `Preservation of types (disabled)` already is here: a `test_case` that skips but still `ignore`s the QCheck test, so it keeps compiling and re-enabling is one line.

Each disabled property is replaced by a unit test on its issue's counterexample:

- **#2128/#2372** — `fun (x::x) -> x`: one engine freshens the duplicate binder, the other doesn't, and `Equality.semantic.exp` doesn't equate the alpha-variants.
- **#2457** — `{ let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }` with the literal bumped: fresh eval substitutes `x` into the residual environment, incremental leaves it a variable.

**#2408** fixes a different confluence cause — uncollapsed casts in indeterminate `if` branches, not binder freshening — so the #2128 pin should still be red after it lands. Both PRs edit this file; happy to rebase on it, or to drop the confluence half here and keep only the #2457 disable.

**#2397** is untouched: "Pattern equivalence" exhausts node's 4 GB heap on ~1 seed in 6, and an OOM kills the process rather than failing a test, so it can't be pinned this way. Wants a lower `~count`/step limit, separately.

```
failed on >= 1 cases:
(6, { type x = (); let _ = 0; type ? = ?; let _ = B; type ? = Bool; type x = ();
      let y = 0.193974; let _ = 1; type y = (); let A = 1261828.579156; let ? = A })
(after 1 shrink steps)
```

Reported to the checks API as `exception raised: test crashed`.

`qcheck random seed: 955690280`, so it should be deterministic:

```
QCHECK_SEED=955690280 bash test/run_node.sh test 'Evaluator.Properties'
```

Worth separating, because the symptom is easy to conflate. #2397 is an OOM that aborts the run, so later groups never execute. This run finished normally:

```
1 failure! in 751.689s. 3752 tests run.
```

3752 is the full count — the same number the run produced locally, where everything passed. So this is one property failing, not a run that died.

- The same commit passed locally: 3752 tests, exit 0 (539.7s), and again on a rebuild.
- The branch's diff is livelit/projector/rendering code. The generators do not produce the term forms it touches.
- Earlier in the same branch's life, two *other* properties in this group failed in about 11 local runs — three distinct properties failing across runs points at the group rather than at any one property.

The shrunk counterexample has the same flavor as #2372 (duplicate binders): `type x = ()` twice, `type ? = ?`, a constructor-shaped binder holding a float (`let A = 1261828.579156`), and `let ? = A`. That is a guess from reading the term, not a diagnosis.

Also in the same family: #2372, #2287.

### Cost so far

A change on this branch was reverted in response to a red build from this group, and the revert turned out to be unnecessary — the failure was the flake, not the change. A red `Evaluator.Properties` currently cannot be distinguished from a real regression without re-running.

### Not verified

- Whether the seed reproduces locally (the machine was busy with a full run when this was written).
- Whether it reproduces on `dev`. #2397 and #2287 both do, so branch-independence is likely but untested here.

title: `ExpToSegment` drops backticks on keyword labels, producing unparseable output
body:
## Description

When `ExpToSegment` prints a labeled tuple whose label is a keyword (`type`, `let`, `fun`, ...), it emits the label bare instead of backtick-quoted. The result is a program that no longer parses, so printing is not round-tripping.

```
(`type` = 3)
```

prints as

```
(type = 3)
```

but `type` is a keyword, so re-parsing that text fails — it comes back as a parse error and an empty hole. All 11 keywords are affected (`fun`, `let`, `in`, `type`, `case`, `test`, `if`, `then`, `else`, `hint`, `module`), in exp, pat, and typ position, and projection loses the quoting the same way (``x.`type` `` prints as `x.type`).

`hazel format` is unaffected because it prints with `PreserveExact`, which reuses the original token text. The bug shows up on every `AutoFormat` path — evaluation results, the stepper, `ExpToSegment.Settings.of_core` and `.editable` — i.e. what the web UI displays for a result value.

## Cause

`Token.quote_label_when_necessary` ([src/haz3lcore/lang/Token.re:280](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/blob/dev/src/haz3lcore/lang/Token.re#L280)) decides quoting from `is_var || is_ctr`:

```reason
let quote_label_when_necessary = (l: string): string =>
  is_var(l) || is_ctr(l) ? l : label_quote(l);
```

`is_var` screens out bools, `undefined`, `_`, and livelits, but not keywords — `is_var("type")` is `true`, so no backticks are added. In label position a keyword can't lex as an identifier, so quoting is in fact necessary there.

title: A function whose body mismatches its expected return type is marked twice
body:
```
let f : Int -> Bool = fun x -> x + 1 in f(1)
```

reports two errors: `x + 1` ("Expecting Bool but got Int") and the whole `fun` ("Expecting Int -> Bool but got Int -> Int"). The second is a consequence of the first, since the function's synthesized type is built from the already-marked body. Only the body should be marked, the way a tuple with a marked component is no longer marked itself after #2502.

Same cascade for a module member checked against its signature, `module M : { let f : Int -> Bool } = { let f = fun x -> x + 1 }`, and for the function shorthand `let f(x) = x + 1` in that position. For the shorthand the second error sits on the synthetic `fun` the desugaring introduces, which has no source span: the CLI prints it as "in term: (fun x -> x + 1)" and the editor cannot highlight it.

Likely fix: in the `Fun` case of statics, when the body carries an expectation-mismatch mark, take the analyzed type for the function instead of synthesizing one from the body (the same mechanism #2502 uses for tuple components, `Mark.is_expectation_mismatch`).

title: Load the Fumola runtime by content hash, and say which one loaded
body:
The consumer side of [Adapton/fumola#69](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/issues/69) — the runtime is published to content-addressed URLs by [Adapton/fumola#76](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/pull/76), and this reads the manifest that names them.

Targets `fumola-livelit-mvp` rather than `dev`, since that is where the Fumola livelit work lives.

**Order does not matter.** An origin with no `runtime.json` is exactly the fallback path. Verified against the live `fumola.org` today, which has none: the loader falls back, reports `fumola.org @ stable`, and evaluates correctly. So this can merge before, after, or independently of the Fumola side.

### The problem

The published runtime is served from stable URLs and GitHub Pages stamps `Cache-Control: max-age=600` on everything with no way to change it. So a Fumola deploy cannot invalidate the 5.6 MB binary a browser already holds, and a livelit can run against a runtime a version behind — which looks like a bug rather than a cache.

### What changed in `prebundle.js`

Reads `<origin>/runtime.json` before importing, and takes the glue and the binary from the directory it names. Both or neither — wasm-bindgen emits them as a matched set and they do not load if their versions disagree, so a half-applied manifest would be worse than ignoring one.

A published origin stays **one** source with one timeout budget rather than becoming two entries; doubling the source count would double the worst case a page waits before reporting the runtime unavailable (currently 90s across three).

### `window.fumola.source()` now says which version

```
"fumola.org @ 290846d3aad19d38"   the current build, by content hash
"fumola.org @ stable"             manifest unreachable; the root pair
"local @ stable"                  your own scripts/build-fumola-wasm.sh
```

Previously unanswerable from a browser, and it is the first question worth asking when a livelit misbehaves for someone and not for you. It also removes the need for a `fumola_version()` export compiled into the wasm — the manifest is the version stamp.

### Verification

Driven in a browser with the **real** bundle (esbuild over `prebundle.js`, same as the dune rule):

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Live `fumola.org` (no manifest today) | falls back, `fumola.org @ stable`, `` `x := 41; get(`x) + 1 `` → 42 |
| Locally published site with a manifest | requests `runtime.json`, then the hashed glue and binary; `source()` reports the hash; → 42 |

Plus `dune build src/web/www/bundled.js`, and `FumolaValue` 54/54, `FumolaSource` 21/21 — though see below on what those actually cover.

### `docs/fumola-runtime-changes.md`

New, and the reason this was looked at. Hazel pins no version of Fumola — no submodule, no revision, no lockfile entry — so **a change merged there reaches every Hazel user without any commit here, and nothing in Hazel's CI notices.** The doc records the dependency precisely (including that the bridge calls only 6 of the runtime's 17 exports, which is what makes "did that Fumola change break us?" a two-minute check), an event log starting with fumola#74, and a four-tier testing methodology.

Its least comfortable finding, stated plainly because green tests are easy to mistake for coverage here: **nothing in either repository tests a Fumola livelit against a live runtime.** `Evaluator.Livelit` skips all four outright; `FumolaValue` and `FumolaSource` feed hand-written JSON fixtures and would pass with the wasm deleted; `prebundle.js` has no test of any kind; there is no headless harness. Those fixtures are the only written record of the two repos' agreement and they are transcribed by hand, so a reply-shape change in Fumola leaves them passing while asserting the old shape. Generating them from the runtime is the first thing that would close it, and needs no browser.

title: Load the Fumola runtime from a list of sources, not one
body:
Groundwork for pointing **fumola.org** at the Fumola Pages site. No behaviour change today.

### Why

`prebundle.js` hard-codes one published URL for the wasm runtime:

```js
glue: "https://adapton.github.io/fumola/fumola_wasm.js",
wasm: "https://adapton.github.io/fumola/fumola_wasm_bg.wasm",
```

Once `Adapton/fumola` takes `fumola.org` as its Pages custom domain, those URLs 301 to `https://fumola.org/...`. A GitHub Pages custom-domain redirect carries **no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header** — verified against a live example (`pytorch.github.io/examples/`, whose org site is CNAME'd to docs.pytorch.org) — and a CORS-mode `import()` must pass the CORS check on *every* hop of a redirect chain, not just the final response. The runtime files themselves do serve `access-control-allow-origin: *`; it's the redirect in front of them that doesn't.

So the old URL works before the switch and fails after; the new one fails before and works after. Neither spans it, which would leave the deployed preview without its published-runtime fallback for as long as the two sides are out of step.

### What

`LOCAL` / `PUBLISHED` become a `SOURCES` list, tried in order — local, then `fumola.org`, then `adapton.github.io` — and the promise chain becomes a loop. Local stays first, so working on Fumola and Hazel together is unchanged. Whichever published URL is live answers; the other fails fast and costs one request.

When every source fails, `loadError` now names all of them and what each said, instead of only the last error.

### After the domain settles

The `adapton.github.io` entry will only ever redirect, and should be dropped.

### Checking it

Open the preview and look at the console: it now logs `runtime loaded from <name>`, and `window.fumola.source()` returns that name. Before the domain moves, expect `adapton.github.io`; after, `fumola.org`.

body:
CI hit a seed-dependent failure of the `Evaluator and stepper are consistent` QCheck property (run 28610859752, on probes-iv — the property and the engines it exercises are identical to dev):

```
Expected: `^^fold(fun (x:: x) -> x)'
Received: `^^fold(fun (x:: x') -> x')'
on `fun (x:: x) -> x` (after 1 shrink steps)
```

One engine freshens the duplicate binder in the cons pattern (`x::x` → `x::x'`), the other doesn't, and `Equality.semantic.exp` doesn't equate the two alpha-variants, so the property fails on whatever run happens to generate a duplicate-binder pattern. The same commit passes the full suite locally under a different seed.

Possible fixes: make `Equality.semantic` alpha-blind for duplicate binders, align the freshening behavior between evaluator and stepper, and/or fix the QCheck seed in CI for determinism.

title: Serve large build assets from outside the Pages size budget
body:
## Context

`hazelgrove/build` holds one directory per branch, and it has outgrown what GitHub Pages will publish. When a build exceeds that, the whole site fails to build, so every branch loses its preview at once — not just the branch that tipped it over.

The scale is audited in **hazelgrove/build#2**: 708 build directories totalling ~7.6 GB, against a 5.1 GB repo. Auto-deploy only ever adds and updates, never prunes, so every branch ever built upstream was still being served, including ones deleted from `hazelgrove/hazel` long ago. That PR removed 136 stale directories (~1.13 GB) — the conservative slice where the source branch is deleted upstream *and* its PR is verifiably merged into `dev` by ancestry rather than by trusting the merged flag.

That work is the accumulation half of the problem, and this issue is the other half: where a branch should put an asset that is genuinely large, so it does not consume the shared budget at all. The two are complementary — pruning reclaims space that should never have been held, while this would keep large artifacts out of the budget in the first place.

## How we got here

This is written up from having caused it, in #2492 (Fumola livelits).

That branch needs a 5 MB WebAssembly runtime in the browser. The first arrangement was to commit the built artifact under `src/web/www`, on the reasoning that branch previews deploy that directory verbatim, so an uncommitted runtime would mean a preview where the feature could not run. That took the branch directory from ~7.9 MB to ~13.4 MB.

**Pages then failed to build the entire site**, on that push and every one after. Not just our branch — `hazel.org/build/dev` and every other preview stopped updating too, because the site is published as a whole. The last successful build had been at 03:25 that morning; the first failure was four seconds after our deploy commit landed.

Diagnosing it took a while, partly because the failure mode is unhelpful: the Pages API reports `Page build failed.` with no detail, one build ran for 18 minutes before failing, and a later one failed in 2 seconds, which made it look like two different problems. Removing the binary and re-deploying did not immediately fix it either, which briefly pointed away from the real cause.

The fix was to stop shipping the artifact inside the preview at all. It is now built by CI in the owning repository, published to GitHub Pages there, and fetched at runtime by the deployed page. The branch directory is back to **7.9 MB**, against `dev` at 7.8 MB.

Two things are worth separating. Committing 5 MB into one preview was a mistake and is fixed. But as hazelgrove/build#2 documents, the repo was already at ~7.6 GB across 708 directories with nothing ever pruned, so the headroom problem is structural and was going to arrive regardless — our binary only chose the moment.

## The finding worth recording

**A GitHub *release asset* cannot serve this purpose.** Release downloads are served without an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, so a browser can never fetch one cross-origin — a page trying to load it fails with a CORS error. This is the obvious first thing to reach for and it is a dead end for anything the browser itself must load.

Verified from a page on a different origin:

| Host | Cross-origin fetch | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Release asset | ❌ no `ACAO` | downloadable by a human, unusable by a page |
| GitHub Pages | ✅ | serves the correct `application/wasm`; stable URL |
| raw.githubusercontent | ✅ | wrong content type; loaders may need a fallback path |
| jsDelivr (`/gh/`) | ✅ | correct type, CDN-cached, serves files committed at a tag |

The working arrangement now in #2492: the artifact is built by CI in the owning repository, published to an orphan `gh-pages` branch there, and fetched by the deployed page. The page prefers a local build when one is present, so working on both repositories at once still behaves, and falls back to the published one otherwise. Nothing binary is tracked in `hazelgrove/hazel`.

## To explore

- **A general way for branch previews to reference large assets** held outside the build repo, so that a branch needing one does not consume the shared size budget. Today this is arranged by hand, per branch.
- **Where such assets should live.** A dedicated assets repository with Pages enabled, an object store, or a CDN in front of either. Whatever it is needs CORS and a sensible content type, which rules out release assets and makes `raw.githubusercontent` awkward.
- **Content addressing.** Naming an asset by hash would let several branches share one copy, and would make a preview reproducible rather than pinned to whatever a mutable branch currently publishes.
- **How this interacts with pruning.** hazelgrove/build#2 began reclaiming space from dead branches, and more is planned. An external asset store has its own lifetime, and an asset outliving every preview that referenced it — or being collected while one still points at it — are both worth thinking about before the two mechanisms exist side by side. Content addressing would help here too: an asset nothing references is then identifiable rather than merely old.
- **Whether the deploy workflow should do it.** At present a developer must arrange external hosting themselves; the workflow could grow a convention, so that a file placed somewhere specific is published outside the preview directory automatically.

title: Type-check the expansion of each user-defined livelit
body:
`user-livelits` does the heavy lifting. This is a small modification on top of it.

Before:

- No `Expansion` type member being looked at.
- No check against this absent member.

Now:

- The type member `Expansion` is required, and so are `Model` and `Action`.
- The check is performed for each expansion, on its output.

The tuple definition form goes with this, having nowhere to declare the types.

### Coming into alignment with livelits in PLDI 2021

**Part 1 — this PR.** The check against the statically named type, performed at the dynamic sites. That is the paper's own strategy rather than an approximation of it: §3.2.5 records that Hazel does not statically check `expand`'s definition, and that the parameterized expansion is instead "validated at each livelit invocation site, with errors reported to the client." With no splices that expansion takes no arguments, so validating it degenerates to checking the expansion at the expansion type.

**Parts 2+ — outside the scope here, and absent from `dev` too.** These introduce:

- the `SpliceRef` primitive type and its operations — `new_splice`, `set_splice` and `eval_splice`, in the paper's `UpdateCmd` and `ViewCmd` monads;
- the quoted AST — `Exp`, an encoding of Hazel's syntax, whose introduction form is quasiquotation, `` `0` `` (§3.2.1);
- `expand` extended to return a pair with that list of `SpliceRef`s, as in Fig. 3 of the [paper](https://hazel.org/papers/livelits-pldi2021.pdf): `expand : Model -> (Exp, List(SpliceRef))`.

The pair is there because "the expansion must treat splices parametrically" (§3.2.5): the first component takes one argument per listed `SpliceRef` and returns the expansion type. Note that `expand` itself stays pure — splices bring the monads, but not to `expand`.

The quotation is entailed by the splices rather than an independent choice. We can do without `Exp` here only because the splice list is empty: a closed expansion need not be code at all, so `expand` returns an ordinary value of the expansion type and application does the work quotation would have done. Splices force the issue, since a parameterized expansion embedding client-site expressions cannot be an ordinary value. (§3 flags the paper's quasiquotation and do notation as presentational sugar rather than implemented Hazel, so both are new surface syntax, not just new library types.)

The paper names one further alternative we are not pursuing: definition-site verification via "a typed quotation system as in, e.g., MetaOCaml." That is a distinct thing from the quasiquotation above — untyped quotation merely introduces `Exp`, whereas typed quotation is what would move Part 1's check from the invocation site to the definition site. The paper notes it is awkward because "the type of the quotation depends on the type of each splice in the splice list."

title: Add function call pattern selectors for function application spines
body:
Implements the `name(` call pattern in the selector language so agents can navigate and edit function call arguments directly (e.g. `authenticate(`, `authenticate ( _ %`, `% authenticate ( _... )`), instead of relying on `#N` chains or `\...` workarounds.

### Selector resolver (`Selector.re`)

- **Tokenizer**: glued tokens like `authenticate(` split into `authenticate` + `(`
- **Call spine matching**: `MatchName` + `(` on `Ap` / `DeferredAp` nodes walks argument slots via the existing sequence-spine machinery (`%`, `_`, `_...`)
- **Subtree search**: `authenticate(` finds nested call sites without requiring `\...`
- **Whole-call focus**: `% authenticate ( _... )` selects the entire call expression
- **Arg-by-value**: `authenticate ( _... % 3` focuses the argument equal to `3`
- **Tuple fallback**: if no call matches, `name(` enters a binder named `name` and walks its definition as a tuple spine (same as `name/ (`)
- **`descend_all`**: recurses into `DeferredAp` argument lists

### Tests (`Test_AgentTools.re`)

15 new tests under `AgentTools.Gaps` covering:
- Multi-arg `Ap`, unary calls, `DeferredAp` deferrals
- Positional navigation, ellipsis, arg-by-value
- Under-binding (`ok = authenticate(`), `\...` descent, whole-call focus
- Tuple fallback (`t(`) and tuple regression (`t/ ( %`)

## Examples

| Program | Selector | Focus |
|---------|----------|-------|
| `let ok = authenticate(3, 4, 5) in ok` | `authenticate(` | `3` |
| same | `authenticate ( _ %` | `4` |
| same | `% authenticate ( _... )` | whole call |
| `let ok = authenticate(_, 4, 5) in ok` | `authenticate(` | deferral `_` |
| `let t = (10, 20, 30) in t` | `t(` | `10` (tuple fallback) |
